World.title: Kazakhstan Temporarily Reduces Oil Production Amid CPC Export Suspension
World.content:
86343

ASTANA — Kazakhstan has temporarily reduced oil production following the suspension of loading operations at the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) marine terminal in the Black Sea, the Energy Ministry said on July 23.

Loading operations at the CPC marine terminal have been temporarily suspended to ensure the safety of vessels, crews and the environment in the Black Sea. All production and technical facilities of the consortium remain fully operational and are ready to resume crude oil shipments as soon as conditions normalize.

“Due to restrictions on oil intake into the pipeline system, oil-producing companies have made a controlled adjustment to daily production levels to prevent storage facilities from reaching capacity. The temporary reduction in oil output is a technological measure aimed at maintaining stable production processes,” reads the ministry’s statement.

The ministry said it is in contact with CPC management, major shippers, shipowners and relevant government agencies. Consultations are ongoing to ensure safe navigation and facilitate the prompt resumption of stable exports of Kazakh oil to global markets.

Reuters reported earlier that Kazakhstan’s oil production had declined following the closure of a Black Sea terminal serving as the country’s main export route for crude oil, which was recently targeted by drone attacks. According to industry sources cited by Reuters, the decline has been notably sharp at the Chevron-led Tengiz field, Kazakhstan’s largest oilfield.

Kazakhstan condemned the drone attacks on civilian vessels transporting oil through the CPC infrastructure on July 17 and 19, describing them as threats to international energy security.

World.title: Kazakhstan Allocates Over $22 Million for KazSat-3R Communications Satellite
World.content:
98180

ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s government has allocated 10.4 billion tenge (US$22.3 million) to begin developing the KazSat-3R communications satellite, which will replace the existing KazSat-3 spacecraft and ensure the uninterrupted operation of the country’s national satellite communications system.

Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov signed the corresponding resolution as part of the implementation of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s directive to strengthen Kazakhstan’s digital infrastructure and expand access to modern telecommunications services, reported the Prime Minister’s press service on July 23.

KazSat-3R will replace the current KazSat-3 satellite, whose planned operational life expires in 2029. The new spacecraft is intended to ensure continuity of national satellite communications services while supporting the long-term development of Kazakhstan’s telecommunications sector.

The project is expected to enhance the reliability of satellite communications and television broadcasting networks, expand internet access in sparsely populated and remote areas, strengthen information security and reinforce the country’s technological sovereignty.

The KazSat satellite system currently provides television broadcasting, data transmission, mobile communications and internet services. It is used by 19 domestic telecommunications operators and government agencies, serving more than two million television subscribers.

The satellite project forms part of broader efforts to modernize Kazakhstan’s digital infrastructure. Over the past two years, high-speed internet coverage has reached 99% of the population, including more than 4,500 rural settlements. Other initiatives include expanding fiber-optic networks in rural areas, implementing the Last Mile project, rolling out 5G, extending mobile coverage along highways and deploying modern satellite technologies.

More than 90% of public services are now available online, while the launch of national supercomputing capacity and the unified QazTech digital platform is intended to support the development of artificial intelligence and the digital economy.

According to the government, KazSat-3R, together with new Earth observation satellite projects, will strengthen Kazakhstan’s space industry and expand its technological capabilities.

World.title: IOC Recognizes Kazakhstan’s Olympic Team Preparation Model as International Best Practice
World.content:
73022

ASTANA – The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has recognized the National Olympic Committee (NOC) of Kazakhstan’s system for preparing Olympic delegations as a Best Practice and recommended it to other National Olympic Committees.

The IOC highlighted Kazakhstan’s Athlete and Team Official Agreements (ATOA), developed by the NOC to complement the IOC’s standard Conditions of Participation (CoP). The agreements are tailored to Kazakhstan’s national legislation and cover a broad range of legal, organizational and operational matters related to participation in the Olympic and Youth Olympic Games, the NOC said on July 22.

The IOC noted the introduction of four separate agreements for athletes, coaches and medical staff, media representatives, and other team officials. The documents establish standardized provisions governing the code of conduct, compliance with IOC regulations, financial terms, the use of personal social media during the Games, official uniform requirements and dispute resolution procedures.

According to the IOC, the agreements also reflect a multidisciplinary approach, drawing on the experience of previous Kazakh Olympic delegation leaders (Chefs de Mission) and contributions from the NOC’s sports, international relations, media, marketing and legal departments.

The IOC described Kazakhstan’s model as an effective example of integrating international standards and the Olympic Charter into national practice. It recommended it for adoption by other National Olympic Committees, recognizing Kazakhstan’s approach as an international best practice.

World.title: Kazakhstan Forms 82 Overseas Polling Stations for Kurultai Elections in August
World.content:
82525

ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry has announced on July 22 the composition of election commissions established at the country’s diplomatic missions abroad to organize voting in the elections of deputies to the Kurultai, scheduled for Aug. 23.

A total of 82 overseas polling stations have been formed at Kazakh embassies, consulates and permanent missions across Europe, Asia, the Middle East, North and South America, Africa and Oceania to ensure voting access for Kazakh citizens residing or staying abroad.

The ministry said the commissions were established in accordance with the Constitutional Law on Elections, the presidential decree calling the elections, and the Central Election Commission’s calendar plan for election preparations.

The published list includes the chairpersons, deputy chairpersons, secretaries and members of all precinct election commissions operating at Kazakhstan’s foreign missions. The measure is aimed at ensuring the openness, transparency and accessibility of the electoral process for citizens outside the country.

World.title: Kazakhstan Dominates Central Asia’s FDI Stock as Uzbekistan Gains Ground
World.content:
591651

ASTANA – Central Asia’s foreign direct investment (FDI) stock rose 3.6% to $235.5 billion in 2025, with Kazakhstan retaining roughly two thirds of the region’s total, according to the latest World Investment Report released by UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD).

Kazakhstan accounted for nearly 66% of Central Asia’s total, solidifying its position as the region’s largest destination for foreign investment. The nation’s FDI stock, which refers to the accumulated value of FDI held in a country, stood at $156.4 billion as of 2025. It went up a little bit from $155.1 billion in 2024. In 2010, the figure was just $82.6 billion.

Uzbekistan, meanwhile, recorded the strongest annual increase from $20.5 billion in 2024 to $26 billion in 2025.

Kazakhstan was a major destination for newly announced large-scale investment projects. One of them relates to a non-ferrous metals project worth more than $12 billion announced by China’s East Hope Group. The report ranks it among the 10 largest greenfield projects announced in developing Asia during the year.

FDI inflows

In terms of FDI inflows, Central Asia received $4.97 billion in 2025, up 12.1% from $4.43 billion in 2024. This is a substantial fall compared to $9.8 billion that the region recorded in 2022.

According to the report, Uzbekistan drove Central Asia’s foreign investment recovery in 2025, attracting nearly $4.4 billion as inflows into Kazakhstan turned negative. Kazakhstan recorded net FDI outflows of $861 million in 2025, compared with net inflows of $227 million a year earlier.

The Kyrgyz Republic posted the region’s fastest percentage increase, with inflows more than doubling to $642 million. Tajikistan’s FDI inflows fell to $86 million, down 70% from $291 million.

According to the report, resource and infrastructure projects in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan featured prominently in the region’s investment activity and project pipeline.

“Investment activity was concentrated in metals and metal products, which together accounted for approximately 45% of total greenfield project activity in the region, followed by energy, transport and storage, chemicals, food processing, and ICT,” reads the report.

Global trends

While global FDI increased by 6% to $1.6 trillion in 2025, this recovery has been uneven and fragile. When excluding financial flows routed through Europe’s largest investment hubs, the increase narrows to 4%.

FDI inflows in developed economies increased by 11% to $723 billion, whereas developing economies received $901 billion in FDI, an increase of 2%.

The largest FDI destination in 2025 was the United States, which received $277 billion. It was also the largest source of FDI last year, followed by Japan and China.

The report indicates that investment activity is becoming more concentrated across regions and sectors.

“Semiconductors, electronics, AI infrastructure, data centres, renewable energy and battery supply chains continued to drive large projects. Project activity was concentrated in China, India, Kazakhstan, Malaysia and the United Arab Emirates, mainly in electronics, digital infrastructure and construction,” it said.

These industries accounted for 44% of global greenfield investment last year, growing from 16% in 2020. Kazakhstan is positioning itself to benefit from the same shift, with major investment plans spanning renewable energy, battery materials, data centers, AI infrastructure and advanced processing of metals and critical minerals, instead of relying solely on extractive industries.

Changing model

Expert Sultan Valikhanov echoes this point in his piece for the EconomyKZ analytical website, cautioning that the rise in global FDI should not be read automatically as a boom in new factories.

“For three decades, the formula was simple: production moved to where labor was cheaper and costs were lower. That allowed dozens of developing countries to join global supply chains and attract factories, logistics hubs and industrial clusters. Capital followed efficiency. The cheaper it was to produce, the greater the chance of attracting an investor,” Valikhanov wrote.

This model is now breaking down. He explained that part of last year’s increase came from intracorporate flows, restructuring and capital routed through international financial centers rather than the expansion of productive capacity.

“What matters, therefore, is not how much capital crossed borders, but where exactly it went,” Valikhanov added.

Stronger domestic capacity

“If most investment is flowing into digital infrastructure and advanced manufacturing, the decisive advantage becomes a country’s ability to support such projects through reliable energy, transport links, engineering talent and a digital ecosystem built around production,” Valikhanov wrote.

That is particularly relevant to Kazakhstan. The headline figures tell only part of the story. What is important is whether that capital went to industries that are capable of generating local value, technology transfer and skilled employment.

UNCTAD also emphasized that countries need to make “deliberate national policy choices,” which among others include “realistic entry points” into changing value chains, and coordinating investment, jobs, supplier policies and infrastructure.

“This will also require renewed international cooperation, with partnerships that balance the resilience that investing countries expect with the development that recipient countries need,” said UNCTAD Acting Secretary-General Pedro Manuel Moreno.

Kazakhstan has increasingly treated trade and investment diplomacy as an instrument of industrial policy, not merely foreign relations. High-level diplomatic visits secure capital, technology, logistics links and access to new value chains. This logic shapes Kazakhstan’s ties with long-established strategic partners such as China and its engagement with newer partners.

“Today, investment follows strategic calculation and industrial policy marked by subsidies, economic security and technological advantage. Governments are competing with new investment policy measures, at a record high in 2025,” said Pedro Manuel Moreno.

He noted that the reshaping of global supply chains is creating opportunities for developing economies to become manufacturing bases, critical-mineral processing hubs and gateways to regional markets. In this context, Kazakhstan is trying to position itself in all three areas by developing transcontinental transport routes, expanding domestic processing of critical raw materials and investing in industrial, technological and skills capacity.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Use Digital Tenge Across Government Spending This August
World.content:
111144

ALMATY – Kazakhstan to begin using the digital tenge in public procurement from August after completing the integration of the digital currency platform with the Finance Ministry’s information systems, reported the Prime Minister’s press service on July 22.

The announcement followed a government meeting chaired by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin, where officials reviewed progress on pilot projects testing the central bank digital currency and discussed challenges to its wider implementation.

According to the ministry, the legal status of the digital tenge platform and its operating procedures have now been established. A total of 340 billion digital tenge (US$626 million) has been issued, with 20 pilot projects completed, 10 underway, and 50 more in preparation.

Beginning in August, the digital tenge will be used for public procurement of goods, including medicines, fuel and lubricants, and other material supplies. Pilot projects cover infrastructure construction, budget lending and subsidies, grant financing, government support measures, public procurement, tax administration, as well as procurement by the National Bank and quasi-state entities.

The government has also introduced mandatory use of the digital tenge for eight categories of budget expenditures covering projects worth more than 100 million tenge (US$184,000).

Officials identified end-to-end traceability of public funds as one of the main challenges to expanding the project. According to the government, while digital tenge transactions can already be tracked from budget allocation to the main contractor, many subcontractors are not yet prepared to conclude smart contracts because current legislation does not require their use.

To address the issue, the ministry has prepared amendments to existing legislation that would establish the legal framework necessary for wider adoption of smart contracts and improve transparency throughout the public spending chain.

World.title: Almaty to Host Central Asia Fintech Summit 2026 in September
World.content:
159353

ALMATY – The Central Asia Fintech Summit (CAFS) 2026 will take place in Almaty on Sept. 11, bringing together financial institutions, fintech companies, regulators, investors and technology leaders to discuss the future of digital finance in Central Asia.

Organized by the National Payment Corporation of Kazakhstan and the National Bank of Kazakhstan, the summit will take place at Tselinny Center of Contemporary Culture from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.

The event is expected to serve as one of the region’s leading platforms for dialogue on financial technologies, digital assets and the development of modern financial infrastructure.

The summit will bring together representatives of the banking sector, fintech firms, international organizations, technology companies, regulators, investors and industry experts to discuss emerging trends and opportunities shaping the regional financial ecosystem.

Building on the momentum of the 2025 edition, organizers say this year’s summit aims to further strengthen cooperation across the industry. Last year’s event marked a shift from a discussion platform to a mechanism for coordinating the fintech sector, resulting in the launch of digital asset initiatives and the signing of strategic industry agreements, including those related to QR payment infrastructure.

The 2025 summit attracted more than 4,000 participants, featured over 80 speakers, and welcomed delegates from more than 30 countries.

World.title: Kazakhstan Reports Record Ice Cream Production in June
World.content:
140114

ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s ice cream production more than doubled in June compared to the same month last year, reaching nearly 20,100 tons, according to new data released by the Bureau of National Statistics. The surge comes as the country’s dairy industry continues to expand, with ice cream among the fastest-growing product categories in the first half of 2026.

The latest figures complement the bureau’s earlier report showing that Kazakhstan’s overall dairy manufacturing output increased by 11.9% in the first six months of the year, driven primarily by strong growth in cheese, butter and ice cream production.

June’s production was 116% higher than a year earlier and almost doubled compared to May. It also exceeded the previous June average of the past five years by 2.5 times and surpassed the previous monthly record of 10,800 tons, set in July 2016, by 85%.

The sharpest increase was recorded in plombir ice cream, a rich, high-butterfat vanilla ice cream, with production reaching 10,200 tons, 3.6 times higher than in June 2025 and nearly three times more than in May. Cream ice cream production also expanded, rising 75% year-on-year and 57% month-on-month to 7,500 tons.

The value of production also increased sharply. Enterprises engaged in ice cream manufacturing produced goods worth 24.3 billion tenge (US$45.4 million) in June, approximately doubling both year-on-year and month-on-month.

The sector has maintained strong momentum since late 2024. Production volumes have recorded annual growth every month since then, averaging 32% year-on-year throughout 2025 and accelerating to around 60% so far in 2026.

According to the Agriculture Ministry, Kazakhstan also became a net exporter of ice cream for the first time in its history last year, with exports exceeding imports.

World.title: ‘Unsolved crimes are being passed off as suicides’: Armenian soldier’s death sparks questions
World.content:
Death of soldier in the Armenian Armed Forces

A serviceman has died at an Armenian military base. Investigators found the body of 20-year-old conscript Narek Torosyan on July 21. The Investigative Committee released only limited information after the incident. It said authorities had opened a criminal case and launched an investigation.

The committee later charged two of Torosyan’s fellow servicemen with driving him to suicide through negligence. One is a junior sergeant and the other a private. Authorities have placed both men under arrest.

The Ministry of Defence has made no public statement about the soldier’s death. Human rights activists and politicians have condemned the ministry’s silence.

Among them was human rights defender Zhanna Aleksanyan, who regularly raises concerns about human rights violations in the armed forces. She wrote on social media that Defence Minister Suren Papikyan ultimately bears responsibility for the lives of servicemen.

“The minister remains strikingly detached when soldiers die. At the end of each year, he tries to downplay the numbers, but no genuine effort exists to reduce the death toll,” she said.

According to official figures, eight servicemen have died since the beginning of 2026.

What we know so far

Armenian media report that Narek came from the town of Charentsavan and was a fourth-year student at the Russian-Armenian University. He hoped to become a sports journalist. The army drafted him in January 2026. Shortly before the incident, he had gone home on leave and visited his family. Reports also identify Chambarak as his duty station.

Authorities have not disclosed where the incident took place or what exactly happened.

According to a version published by several local media outlets, other servicemen severely beat the soldier before he took his own life.

Charentsavan Mayor Hakob Shahgeldyan also told reporters that, according to the information available to him, Narek had died by suicide. However, the mayor provided no further details.

Comments

Human rights activist Zhanna Aleksanyan wrote:

“The Ministry of Defence remains silent about the death of 20-year-old serviceman Narek Torosyan.

The minister has still offered no explanation or clarification. Did he visit the military unit to find out what happened and why? I am certain he did not. He bears responsibility for the life of every serviceman, and he is accountable to both their families and society.

I cannot accept the ‘suicide’ version circulating in the media. Journalists may learn that a serviceman has died, but they cannot know the circumstances of his death. Law enforcement agencies often leak such versions to the press. They later use those same reports to support their own conclusion that it was ‘suicide.’

And in the army, most ‘suicides’ are in fact unsolved murders.”

Tigran Abrahamyan, an opposition MP from the I Have Honour alliance, wrote on social media:

“Soldier Narek Torosyan, who died following the incident at the Chambarak military base, was my student. […]

Narek was a kind, gentle person with outstanding personal qualities. Both students and lecturers respected and cared for him.

Given the sensitivity of the case, I do not want to comment on the different versions or discuss the information available to me.

One thing is clear, however. The state has failed to ensure proper discipline, maintain a healthy psychological environment in military units, and provide effective oversight. That failure ultimately leads to incidents like this.

The authorities must carry out an objective and comprehensive investigation and take steps to prevent similar tragedies in the future.”

Mané Tandilyan, founder of the Country to Live party, said:

“Do not say that incidents like this are inevitable in the army. We must not accept such an attitude. After so many losses, it is unacceptable that we continue to lose our young people in peacetime.

How do officers demonstrate accountability? How has violence and cruelty become so deeply rooted among 18- to 20-year-olds that it repeatedly leads to deaths? What is the army doing to foster mutual respect, discipline and responsibility?

What is especially alarming is that intolerance and aggression are becoming increasingly visible in society. And yes, much of the responsibility lies with the country’s top leadership, which speaks to society in a language that fuels division, hostility and hatred. That atmosphere eventually seeps into people’s everyday relationships.

We must overcome this nightmare. Let us each begin with the people around us.”

Death of soldier in the Armenian Armed Forces

World.title: Historic home of Abkhaz literary patriarch Dmitry Gulia destroyed in Abkhazia
World.content:
Dmitry Gulia’s dacha destroyed in Abkhazia

An outcry has erupted in Abkhazia after reports emerged that a businessman had seized and demolished historic seaside dachas belonging to Dmitry Gulia, regarded as the patriarch of Abkhaz literature, and Konstantin Simonov, the renowned Soviet writer.

The two properties were located in the coastal settlement of Agudzera. According to reports circulating on social media, the owner of a neighbouring beachfront plot decided to expand his estate by taking over the writers’ properties. The buildings were demolished, and the entire site was levelled with heavy machinery.

The dacha was built in 1957 by the prominent Soviet writer Georgy Gulia for his father, Dmitry Gulia, the founder of Abkhaz literature.

According to Dmitry Gulia’s granddaughter, Tatyana Gulia, he was already elderly and in poor health, and doctors advised him to live by the sea. Dmitry Gulia spent the last three years of his life in the modest single-storey house, which had a veranda and three rooms. He also died there.

Agudzera, Abkhazia. Family members and guests of writer Georgy Gulia at the family dacha, 1970s. Photo from the Gulia House Museum’s Instagram account.

The public outcry forced the Abkhaz authorities to state that “a mistake had been made and there was no threat of the land being seized.”

Next to the Gulia house stood the dacha of another prominent Soviet writer, Konstantin Simonov, who was a close friend of Georgy Gulia. Before his death in 1979, Simonov bequeathed the property to the Gulia family.

During the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war, both writers’ dachas were looted and partially destroyed. After the war, staff from the Dmitry Gulia Museum helped maintain the two buildings.

Tatyana Gulia discovered that the land had been taken over while visiting the cemetery in Gulripsh, where her grandmother is buried. She wrote on social media:

“We suddenly saw a bulldozer driving across our property, leveling everything to the ground, despite the memorial plaque that had been installed there by the Dmitry Gulia Museum.”

After public outrage mounted, Aslan Ankvab, the head of the Agudzera village administration, called the Gulia family to say that officials had reviewed all the documents and confirmed that both the land and the house remained the property of the Gulia family.

“The remains of the house have been destroyed, but the land itself has been preserved. The authorities have decided to describe what happened as a misunderstanding,” Tatyana Gulia later wrote.

JAMnews reserves the right to delete comments it considers to be offensive, inflammatory, threatening or otherwise unacceptable.



Dmitry Gulia’s dacha destroyed in Abkhazia

World.title: The Belarus factor: Belarusians fighting for Ukraine on Lukashenko’s rule, the threat of war and Russian manipulation
World.content:
Belarusians serving in Ukraine’s Armed Forces

Svytiaz / hromadske

How realistic is the prospect of a new Russian offensive launched from Belarusian territory? Would Alexander Lukashenko send the Belarusian army into Ukraine? Should Kyiv strike Belarusian oil refineries that help sustain Russia’s war effort? And what do Belarusians serving in Ukraine’s Armed Forces think?

hromadske spoke with fighters from the Kastus Kalinouski Regiment. One serviceman, who goes by the call sign Hetman, speaks Ukrainian because he comes from a family of ethnic Ukrainians from the Brest region. Three of his comrades speak Belarusian.

The fighters do not disclose their names or any identifying details that could allow the Belarusian authorities to identify them. Their relatives remain in Belarus, where security officers have already carried out searches of their homes, threatened family members and subjected them to questioning.

All of those interviewed know firsthand what Belarusian prisons and pretrial detention centers are like. Some have been held there, while others narrowly avoided imprisonment. For them, joining the Kastus Kalinouski Regiment became a continuation of their struggle against Alexander Lukashenko’s regime.

An hromadske report.

A country of political prisoners

According to a fighter with the call sign Salam, meaningful political and civic activism in Belarus has become virtually impossible because of the regime’s pervasive control.

“Lukashenko seems to have taken inspiration from Orwell’s 1984. Any attempt by people to organize independently is crushed,” he says.

Since 2020, around half a million people have left Belarus. Between 40,000 and 60,000 Belarusians have been subjected to political repression, according to Salam. That has included arbitrary detention, torture, sexual violence and lengthy prison sentences.

According to Salam, people released from prison are often forced into exile. Independent civil society organizations have been dismantled, while independent media outlets have been designated as “extremist organizations.” Even subscribing to an independent Telegram channel, he says, can result in 30 days of detention and torture.

Salam also claims that simply speaking Belarusian in public can lead to punishment, as the authorities may interpret it as an act of political protest.

Salam on the Bakhmut front, 2023. Photo from Salam’s personal archive

According to Algerd, more than 5,000 opponents of the Lukashenko regime have been imprisoned on politically motivated charges. The regiment has also documented around 400 cases of people persecuted for supporting Ukraine. The reasons include donating to Ukraine’s Armed Forces and having links to the Belarusian Hajun monitoring project, which tracked the deployment and movement of Russian troops.

He says prison sentences have become somewhat less severe than they were in 2020 and during the early stages of Russia’s full-scale invasion. Even so, those convicted still face terms of 10 to 15 years. People accused of sabotaging railways or taking part in the attack on the Machulishchy air base have received sentences of 20 years or more.

Hetman sums up the situation succinctly: “The screws have been tightened. The authorities control everything—and Russia controls the authorities.”

Algerd near Bakhmut, September 2023. Photo from Algerd’s personal archive

What the Belarusian opposition can do

During the 2020 protests, some Ukrainians mocked the largely peaceful nature of the demonstrations in Belarus. Algerd believes that perception tells only part of the story.

“Television showed you white socks, but not the violent clashes with the security forces,” he says. “In Pinsk, for example, protesters fought back against OMON riot police. Across the country, up to a million people took part in the protests.”

According to Algerd, the Belarusian protest movement unfolded under very different conditions from Ukraine’s Maidan.

“Ukraine had a genuine political opposition and relatively democratic institutions. By 2020, Lukashenko had already consolidated control over the KGB, the army and the rest of the security apparatus,” he says.

In the aftermath of the protests, the regime carried out another sweeping crackdown on its political opponents. Some opposition figures remain behind bars, others have gone into exile, and many have abandoned public political activity altogether.

“Six years have passed since the last mass protests. The Belarusian opposition is fragmented and lacks unity,” Hetman says.

According to Algerd, the Belarusian protest movement unfolded under very different conditions from Ukraine’s Maidan.

“Ukraine had a genuine political opposition and relatively democratic institutions. By 2020, Lukashenko had already consolidated control over the KGB, the army and the rest of the security apparatus,” he says.

In the aftermath of the protests, the regime carried out another sweeping crackdown on its political opponents. Some opposition figures remain behind bars, others have gone into exile, and many have abandoned public political activity altogether.

“Six years have passed since the last mass protests. The Belarusian opposition is fragmented and lacks unity,” Hetman says.

Algerd near Kupiansk, October 2023. Photo from Algerd’s personal archive.

Algerd sees the Belarusian opposition’s value in a different light. In his view, Western governments recognize Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya as the legitimate representative of democratic Belarus, and that international standing should be put to use.

Svytiaz, however, criticizes the Ukrainian authorities for the warm reception Tsikhanouskaya received in Kyiv. He notes that Belarusian volunteers—who have been fighting and suffering losses in Ukraine for years—have never been received at such a high official level.

“In 2020, people voted for Tsikhanouskaya above all because they wanted Lukashenko out. She did not have a fully developed political platform, and it remains unclear what her government would actually look like if she came to power. Yet Ukraine welcomed her at the highest official level, while Belarusian volunteers have never received such recognition. That is a serious miscalculation by the Ukrainian authorities,” Svytiaz says.

In his view, Kyiv should develop a separate strategy for engaging with Belarusian volunteers fighting on Ukraine’s side.

Salam near Zaporizhzhia, 2026. Photo from Salam’s personal archive.

Will the Belarusian army attack Ukraine?

Five years into the war, Ukraine continues to fortify its border with Belarus. Kyiv has not ruled out the possibility that Russia could once again use Belarusian territory to launch an offensive.

Svytiaz believes such a scenario remains possible because “anything can be expected from Moscow.” At the same time, he says Alexander Lukashenko is likely to avoid direct involvement if he can. Yet Belarus’s dependence on the Kremlin means Russia could ultimately force his hand.

Algerd, however, argues that it is not currently in Moscow’s interest to draw Belarus directly into the fighting.

“Russia is already using Belarusian factories to produce and repair military equipment,” he says. “It also tests military hardware there and trains mobilized troops.”

Algerd with fellow soldiers near Kupiansk, December 2023. Photo from Algerd’s personal archive

Salam views the issue primarily through a political lens. In his opinion, direct participation in the war would be politically suicidal for Alexander Lukashenko. For decades, his propaganda has been built around a single promise: that he would keep Belarus out of war.

“In 2015, Lukashenko told Belarusians: If you want a war like the one in Ukraine, vote for the opposition. After Russia’s full-scale invasion, he repeated that the war was the consequence of Ukraine’s pro-European course,” Salam says.

He also argues that in February 2022, Lukashenko believed Russia would quickly defeat Ukraine and capture Kyiv within three days. Today, however, Salam believes he no longer has the same confidence in Russia’s military strength. “That’s why Lukashenko has no desire to join a losing war,” he says.

Algerd on Christmas Eve 2024, Zaporizhzhia front. Photo from Algerd’s personal archive.

The fighters point to three additional factors they believe make direct Belarusian involvement less likely: Vladimir Putin’s distrust of Belarusians, widespread anti-war sentiment within Belarusian society, and the army’s limited combat capability.

According to Algerd, in 2022 Russian commanders did not allow Belarusian doctors to treat wounded Russian soldiers. Instead, medical personnel were brought in from Russia.

He also argues that Putin did not insist on deploying the Belarusian army during the invasion because he understood how limited Lukashenko’s support was inside Belarus.

Salam in the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone, April 2022. Photo from Salam’s personal archive

Salam believes that most Belarusians do not want war and are unwilling to fight for Lukashenko. While part of society has embraced Russian propaganda, he argues that the risk of widespread resistance would remain high if Belarus were drawn directly into the conflict.

Hetman offers another reason why Lukashenko may hesitate: arming large numbers of people could ultimately threaten his own rule if those weapons were turned against the regime.

The fighters also give a bleak assessment of the Belarusian military, describing its combat readiness as extremely poor.

Hetman near Pokrovsk. Photo from Hetman’s personal archive

“One out of ten,” Hetman says, rating the Belarusian army’s combat capability on a ten-point scale.

Salam adds that the military has virtually no real combat experience.

Nor, the fighters note, has Ukraine encountered the latest Belarusian weapons that Minsk periodically claims to have developed. It is also unclear whether the Belarusian army is prepared for modern warfare, where drones play a central role on the battlefield.

Belarus is estimated to have a theoretical mobilization reserve of around 400,000 people. Svytiaz, however, doubts that the authorities could actually send them to the front.

“They would either leave the country or protest,” he says. “Forcing them to fight would require another wave of repression. That would be costly and difficult—and Belarusian prisons are already overcrowded.”

Could Ukraine strike Belarus?

Belarusian oil refineries continue to supply petroleum products to Russia. Russian troops use Belarusian military training grounds, and Moscow also relies on Belarusian infrastructure to help guide attack drones toward Ukraine.

That raises the question of whether Ukraine would be justified in targeting such facilities.

Hetman considers Belarus a co-aggressor alongside Russia since 2022. In his view, Ukraine would have the right to strike if Belarusian territory were once again used to launch a ground offensive or missile attacks.

For now, however, he says no such aggression is taking place. As a result, he sees no legal or military justification for Ukrainian strikes on Belarusian oil refineries.

Salam near Zaporizhzhia, 2025. From Salam’s personal archive

Salam also warns against deploying Ukrainian ground forces into Belarus. Such an operation, he argues, would require diverting troops from other sections of the front, while holding captured territory would create major logistical challenges.

He also points to China’s position. Beijing has invested heavily in Belarus and views the country as a key link in its overland trade corridor to Europe. China, he says, has little interest in seeing that route disrupted by war.

At the same time, Salam says Ukraine could justify limited strikes against facilities that directly support Russia’s military operations — for example, communication relay stations used to guide or coordinate drone attacks.

Sviatsiaz believes Ukraine has the technical capability to destroy the oil refineries in Mazyr and Navapolatsk.

But doing so, he argues, would deprive Belarus of fuel for its domestic market and deepen the country’s dependence on Russia. The Kremlin could then use fuel supplies as another lever of pressure on Minsk.

“Ukraine must act wisely,” Sviatsiaz says.

Salam, for his part, hopes Ukrainian strikes on Belarus never become necessary. He does not want to see the war spread onto the territory of his own country.

Fighters from the Kalinouski Regiment in a dugout near Bakhmut, 2022. From Salam’s personal archive.

When could the Kalinouski regiment return to Belarus?

In March 2022, Alhierd was told that the Belarusian unit would fight for Ukraine first. One day, he says, it might also fight for Belarus.

For now, however, he believes such an operation would be pointless. Belarus, in his view, remains firmly under Russia’s control.

He argues that if Moscow is defeated, one condition of any capitulation should be the withdrawal of Russian forces from Belarus. Only then, he says, could Alyaksandr Lukashenka be presented with an ultimatum: hand over power peacefully or face the dismantling of his regime by force. In that scenario, the Kalinouski Regiment could play a role.

Salam identifies two circumstances under which the regiment might enter Belarus. The first would be the outbreak of new mass anti-government protests requiring armed support. The second would be Belarus’s direct entry into the war against Ukraine.

Sviatsiaz says the prospects for a peaceful transfer of power ultimately depend on developments in Russia. Lukashenka’s government, he argues, survives primarily because of Moscow’s backing.

“Belarusians are fighting Russia in Ukraine to weaken it and bring Belarus’s liberation closer,” he says.

Alhierd believes there is little Ukraine can realistically do inside Belarus at this stage. From Alhierd’s personal archive

Why they keep fighting

According to the interviewees, the Kalinouski Regiment has not recorded a single case of unauthorized abandonment of duty. Its fighters, they say, understood exactly what they were signing up for and why they chose to fight.

If a Belarusian volunteer is killed, however, the soldier’s family is not eligible for Ukraine’s standard compensation payment of 15 million hryvnias.

Capture or disappearance creates additional risks. Relatives who remain in Belarus cannot report a missing family member to the authorities or provide DNA samples for identification, as doing so could expose their connection to a volunteer fighting for Ukraine.

Despite those risks, the regiment’s fighters continue to serve. They also raise money to support veterans of the unit, many of whom struggle to obtain state assistance.

“Would I still fight for Ukraine if I received no combat pay and no compensation for being wounded? I think I would. Money does not change the purpose of this struggle. I have a duty to help liberate Ukraine from Russian occupation.

For Belarus, this is of fundamental importance, because it too remains under Russian occupation and must become free,” Hetman says.

He believes many Belarusians take pride in the Kalinouski Regiment’s fighters. If a historic opportunity to return to Belarus ever emerges, he says, the unit would have the backing of a significant share of the country’s population.

This article was produced with the support of the Media Network.

exchange

World.title: Armenian rights lawyer files ECHR complaint over Ruben Vardanyan’s 20-year jail sentence in Baku
World.content:
ECHR complaint over Vardanyan case

Human rights lawyer Siranush Sahakyan has filed a complaint with the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) over the case of Ruben Vardanyan, the former state minister of the former unrecognised Nagorno-Karabakh Republic. She said she would represent Vardanyan before the court. Sahakyan has represented Armenian detainees at the ECHR for many years.

“The application sets out in detail violations of eight articles of the European Convention on Human Rights, supported by comprehensive legal and factual arguments,” Sahakyan said in a statement shared with the media and posted on social media.

Vardanyan is one of 19 Armenians still held in Azerbaijani prisons. In February 2026, a military court in Baku sentenced him to 20 years in prison.

According to Sahakyan, the defence was only recently able to obtain the court’s written judgment, which was required before an application could be submitted to the ECHR. She said Azerbaijan had withheld the ruling until then, which is why the complaint was filed only on 19 July.

The court found Vardanyan guilty of a number of serious offences, including waging war, financing terrorism and deportation.

Armenian rights groups, however, have described the trial in Baku as “political rather than legal”. Vardanyan himself called the proceedings “a farce” and “a mockery of justice”. During the hearings, he instructed his lawyer not to present arguments in his defence.

“It is impossible to protect rights in a system that fundamentally denies the right to a fair trial. That is why Ruben Vardanyan decided to continue his fight for justice through international legal mechanisms,” Sahakyan said.

Details of Vardanyan case

In her statement, Sahakyan disclosed further details of the case. She said the military court in Baku did not read out the full verdict. Now that Vardanyan’s family has passed the written judgment to his lawyers, it has become clear that he was convicted on 41 counts under 21 articles of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code.

According to Sahakyan, the judgment does not substantiate Vardanyan’s personal criminal responsibility with facts or evidence.

“Instead, the court concluded that the ‘criminal organisation’ – the leadership of the self-proclaimed Republic of Artsakh – had been operating in Nagorno-Karabakh since 1988. It also found that Vardanyan joined this ‘organisation’ in December 2020, although he was living in Moscow at the time.”

She also said the court treated Vardanyan’s appointment to a civilian administrative post as a violent seizure of power. His commercial and charitable activities were classified as illegal entrepreneurship and financing terrorism, while his entry into Nagorno-Karabakh via the Lachin Corridor was deemed an illegal crossing of Azerbaijan‘s state border.

Sahakyan said Vardanyan had not appealed against the verdict because he regarded the trial as staged and pre-planned, and considered all domestic legal remedies ineffective.

Background

On 17 February, a military court in Baku sentenced Russian-Armenian businessman, billionaire and philanthropist Ruben Vardanyan to 20 years in prison. His case was heard separately from those of the former leadership of Nagorno-Karabakh.

A month after the verdict, Vardanyan’s family said he had tried to raise concerns with Azerbaijan’s Human Rights Commissioner, Sabina Aliyeva, during a phone call with relatives, but the call was cut off.

The family has repeatedly appealed to the international community, saying that neither Vardanyan nor the other Armenian detainees in Azerbaijan have access to institutional protection. They argue that the country lacks independent human rights protection mechanisms. They have also noted that the International Committee of the Red Cross, which had facilitated contact between detainees and their families, has ceased operations in Azerbaijan.

On 5 February, two weeks before Vardanyan’s sentence was announced, an Azerbaijani court handed life sentences to several other former Nagorno-Karabakh leaders, including former President Arayik Harutyunyan, former Defence Army commander Levon Mnatsakanyan, his deputy Davit Manukyan, former parliament speaker Davit Ishkhanyan and former Foreign Minister Davit Babayan. Former presidents Arkady Ghukasyan and Bako Sahakyan were sentenced to 20 years in prison.

All of the detainees faced a range of serious charges, including terrorism and genocide. Ghukasyan and Sahakyan received lighter sentences because they are over 65, and Azerbaijani law does not allow life imprisonment for people above that age.

Independent media and human rights observers were not allowed to attend the trials. Information about the proceedings was published by Azerbaijani state and pro-government media.

World.title: One minor killed, three injured in shooting in central Tbilisi
World.content:
Shooting in central Tbilisi

Late on July 22, four people, including two minors, were injured in a shooting on Vera, a central street in Tbilisi. All were taken to hospital. One of the minors died shortly after being admitted, Irakli Pirtskhalaishvili, a doctor at the clinic, told reporters.

Georgia’s Interior Ministry confirmed the incident, saying one person had been arrested in connection with it. The suspect has been charged with using a firearm and wounding four people.

He attempted to flee the scene but was detained after a police chase. According to the ministry, the suspect resisted arrest with a weapon and “sustained finger injuries during the arrest.”

The investigation is being conducted under Articles 19 and 109 of Georgia’s Criminal Code (attempted murder), which carry a penalty of up to 20 years in prison or life imprisonment.

Many witnesses to the shooting: what they say

The shooting took place in central Tbilisi, at the intersection of Akaki Shanidze and Akaki Khorava streets. The area was crowded at the time of the incident.

Eyewitness Elene Koridze wrote on social media that three young men sitting in a car “were shot simply because they were laughing.”

“About an hour ago, right outside my home, a man opened fire on three 17- and 18-year-old boys sitting in a car simply because they were laughing. He then also shot a woman who was nearby. He was quickly apprehended.

It was clear this was neither a premeditated attack nor an act of personal revenge. This is not just an isolated serious crime to which the police responded quickly, but a direct reflection of the reality we live in,” Koridze wrote.

Another eyewitness, Tiko Kvaliashvili, said:

“I was walking home when I saw a crowd on Shanidze Street and went over. Two patrol cars arrived, people started shouting, and someone was running. One boy was unconscious in the car, while two others were in shock. I gave them first aid as best I could. One had been shot in the arm, the other in the shoulder. I don’t know why they were shot.”

The son of journalist Eka Kvesitadze also witnessed the incident. She said it happened near their home while her son was out walking the dog.

“Someone had shot several minors. They were lying there covered in blood,” another witness wrote.

Witnesses also told reporters that a nearby parked red Alfa Romeo had around a dozen bullet holes.

As of now, Interior Ministry has not released any additional details.

World.title: Pro-EU protester Onise Okriashvili attacked in Tbilisi after disinformation campaign
World.content:
Georgia protester Onise Okriashvili beaten

Stand-up comedian Onise Okriashvili, an active participant in Georgia’s pro-European protests that have been ongoing for nearly two years, was brutally beaten by three people late on July 22 outside his home in Tbilisi’s Vake district.

Before the attack, Okriashvili had become the target of a disinformation campaign by pro-government media. Based on the context of the attack, this appears to have been the reason behind the assault.

A video of the attack, recorded by eyewitnesses, has spread on social media.

The footage shows three young men brutally beating Onise. “You insulted Nodar Dumbadze (a classic of Georgian literature), how dare you, bastard?” the attackers are heard saying to him.

Onise Okriashvili can be heard calling for help. Several people are nearby, but they do not dare approach him. The desperate screams of a woman trying to stop the attackers can also be heard.

Who is Onise Okriashvili and why did he become a target of propaganda?

Onise Okriashvili is known for his criticism of the ruling Georgian Dream party on social media. He also regularly organises solo protests aimed at drawing public attention — appearing with relevant posters in places where large numbers of people gather, including on public transport.

“Only their children study in Europe” — reads the sign held by Onise Okriashvili during one of his solo protests. Photo from the activist’s social media page

In recent days, the activist has become the target of a disinformation campaign by pro-government TV channels. They have repeatedly aired a fragment from a comedy show Punchline Therapy, in which he uses a vulgar expression while referring to Nodar Dumbadze, a classic of Georgian literature.

The fragment was shown without context, making it appear as if Okriashvili was directly insulting the writer.

On July 19, the comedian recorded a video in which he said:

“I apologise that in this video I am not talking about more important events in the country. Young people my age are dying every day because of drug use; there are political prisoners in the country; emigration is sharply increasing, and these emigrants have been deprived of the right to vote in elections, along with many other problems.

But for the third day now, Georgian Dream’s propaganda machine has been using all its resources to turn people against me. Here is an example of the video they are using to try to discredit me.“

The conversation in the video excerpt goes:

‘Is there someone you cannot stand?’ ‘What if I say Nodar Dumbadze? (vulgar expression) I will only name our government, no one else.’

“During a performance, we speak hypothetically and can say the most absurd thing that comes to mind at that moment.

This video clearly shows that I am, of course, not insulting (Nodar Dumbadze), but speaking only hypothetically, deliberately using the most absurd example that came to mind at that moment. Comedy often works exactly this way — it uses unexpected twists. That is why the audience laughs at that moment.”

“Just today we were discussing filing a lawsuit against the propaganda media for spreading defamatory claims, and today Onise was attacked,” his wife, Mariam Samushia, told journalists.

She said she heard shouting in the street in the evening. Since Onise had become a target of a propaganda campaign in recent days, she called him to warn him. Only later did she realise that her husband had been attacked.

“This is artificially created hatred,” she said.

The Interior Ministry said a criminal case had been opened over the attack on Onise Okriashvili under Article 126 of Georgia’s Criminal Code (violence). According to reports, one of the attackers has been taken to a police station and is being questioned.

News in Georgia

World.title: Chechnya’s recruitment machine: How Kadyrov sustains his forces by enlisting civilians
World.content:
Kadyrov’s Forces in Ukraine

An investigation by Novaya Gazeta Europe shows how the war has reshaped the system of power in Chechnya.

Ramzan Kadyrov has significantly expanded the number of armed units under his control. But his most loyal formations are largely kept away from the front lines.

Instead, combat losses are replenished with ordinary residents of the republic, who are often pressured into signing military contracts.

For the investigation, journalists interviewed 178 Chechen families who lost relatives in the war, as well as current and former servicemen. Their reporting examines how Chechnya’s recruitment system operates and reveals the true scale of its wartime losses.

Kadyrov’s forces

Over the course of the war, five new regiments and five battalions have been established in Chechnya. Formally, they are part of Russia’s Defense Ministry and the National Guard. In practice, however, Kadyrov determines key personnel appointments, where the units are deployed and how extensively they are involved in combat.

According to figures provided by Kadyrov, the number of security personnel in Chechnya has grown from 4,800 in 2003 to 36,243 today. At the start of 2022, before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, those forces numbered roughly 16,000 to 18,000. That means Chechnya’s security apparatus has approximately doubled in size over the course of the three-year war.

The human rights group Memorial argues that the expansion amounts to the strengthening of Kadyrov’s personal army. But a source in Chechnya’s regional office of the Federal Security Service offered a different explanation. According to the source, Kadyrov became trapped by the image of being “Putin’s chief foot soldier.” While he continued to create new units, he also sought to shield his most loyal security personnel from frontline combat.

At first, the authorities attracted recruits with high salaries. They then began actively recruiting people from other parts of Russia. Later, military service was opened to unemployed residents of Chechnya. As the flow of volunteers dwindled, the authorities increasingly turned to coercion.

The safe rear ended in the Kursk region

In 2023, Kadyrov secured the deployment of several Chechen units to the Russian border regions of Bryansk, Kursk and Belgorod. At the time, these areas were considered relatively safe rear positions, allowing Kadyrov’s forces to be pulled back from the most intense sections of the front.

That changed on Aug. 6, 2024, when Ukrainian troops crossed into the Kursk region. The Akhmat-Chechnya Regiment, which had been guarding the border, offered little visible resistance. Its personnel abandoned their positions, and some were surrounded and taken prisoner.

The border regions subsequently became the scene of heavy fighting involving the Akhmat special forces, the West Akhmat Battalion and the Akhmat-Chechnya Regiment. One Akhmat commander claimed that Apti Alaudinov’s unit alone suffered more than 1,500 killed and wounded.

Security forces are shielded, civilians sent to the front

After the fighting in the Kursk region, Kadyrov moved to reduce the involvement of key National Guard units in the war. Much of the burden was shifted instead to formations under Russia’s Defense Ministry.

Sources interviewed by the publication say the decision was driven by the need to preserve the foundations of Kadyrov’s rule. His grip on power depends on the loyalty of the republic’s security forces. A prolonged war depletes that resource faster than the Chechen leadership can replace it.

A telling example is the National Guard’s Baysangur Benoevsky Battalion. It is overseen by Adam Kadyrov, the 18-year-old son and presumed heir of the Chechen leader. The battalion has been equipped with modern weapons, its own training ground and a well-funded infrastructure. Its personnel signed contracts that предусматривают service in the war. Yet the unit has remained almost entirely in Chechnya, where it focuses on training.

Another National Guard unit, the Sheikh Mansur Battalion, was deployed to the front in December 2023 and has been engaged in combat ever since.

According to the investigation, the Baysangur Battalion is effectively financed with federal funds allocated for the war while serving as the Kadyrov family’s personal security reserve.

Coerced recruitment

Since the autumn of 2024, the Chechen authorities have carried out a large-scale campaign of forced recruitment. Kadyrov publicly proposed sending what he called “troubled youth” to the front. District police departments were then assigned monthly recruitment quotas of between 25 and 50 people.

Those detained are taken to collection centers in Sernovodsk and at the Khankala military base. According to testimonies from recruits and their relatives, they are held under guard, given inadequate food and receive little to no military training. Some are sent without proper uniforms or equipment, receiving weapons only after they reach the front.

People can be sent to the front for reasons as minor as a street fight, a traffic violation, driving without insurance, tinted car windows or unpaid utility bills. Others are detained for subscribing to opposition channels or for political posts found on their phones. In some cases, relatives are offered the chance to pay for a detainee’s release or to find other “volunteers” to take their place.

According to the journalists’ estimates, 67 such raids were carried out across Chechnya between October 2024 and May 2025.

Hidden casualties

The Chechen authorities prohibit the publication of information about those killed in the war. Families are often instructed to bury relatives at night and to forgo the traditional multi-day mourning rituals. As a result, publicly available casualty lists capture only a fraction of the true death toll.

Officially, around 500 residents of Chechnya have been confirmed killed. But a source in the republic’s government told the investigators that more than 2,300 deaths have been verified internally. Another roughly 1,000 people are listed as missing in action.

Of the 183 fatalities documented by the journalists, 113 were sent to the war after October 2024. Of those, 97 had signed military contracts under coercion. The average time between deployment and death was about two months. Only 84 of the 178 families interviewed were able to recover and bury the bodies of their relatives.

The investigation identifies a fundamental shift in Kadyrov’s approach. At the start of the war, he deployed members of the security forces while portraying those forcibly recruited as volunteers. Now, his most loyal units are kept inside Chechnya, while civilians are openly treated as expendable manpower.

The authors argue that this marks a troubling precedent. Repressive practices first tested in Chechnya have often, over time, spread to the rest of Russia.
