World.title: Aliyev confirms secret Russia–Germany talks in Baku during Berlin visit, urges Europe to invest in Azerbaijan
World.content:
Ilham Aliyev’s Berlin briefing

At a joint press conference with Friedrich Merz in Berlin on 21 July, Ilham Aliyev appeared to be addressing three different audiences at once.

To Berlin, he signalled that Azerbaijan does not intend to serve as a venue for other countries’ secret diplomacy. To Brussels, he argued that if Europe wants more Azerbaijani gas, it should also help finance pipelines and interconnectors. And to Moscow and Kyiv, Aliyev sought to demonstrate that Baku remains committed to its multi-vector foreign policy while insisting on setting its own rules.

A strategic agenda signed later that day formally enshrined this political course.

Secret meeting in Baku: what is known and what remains speculation

According to Aliyev, after The Times published its report, the Azerbaijani authorities checked records held by the State Border Service and confirmed that Ronald Pofalla and Matthias Platzeck arrived in Baku from Berlin on 12 July and left on 14 July. During the same period, Viktor Zubkov and Valery Fadeyev flew to Baku from Moscow.

Aliyev said Azerbaijan had received no prior notification from either Germany or Russia and that “Azerbaijan’s territory was used without the knowledge of the authorities”. He stressed that Baku had no confirmed information about the substance of the meeting, but said the travel records suggested that such a meeting could have taken place. He added that if its purpose had been to help end Russia’s war against Ukraine, Azerbaijan could only welcome such efforts.

Merz, for his part, denied any involvement by the German government, saying he had no knowledge of such a meeting.

Investigations by German media describe the contacts as an informal continuation of the Petersburg Dialogue. According to ARD/RBB and Die Zeit, Baku has hosted unofficial meetings since 2024 between former German politicians and figures close to Vladimir Putin.

RBB reported that German security agencies view the meetings as a possible Russian influence operation. Roderich Kiesewetter, a member of the CDU, described them as “shadow diplomacy” that undermines Germany’s position on Ukraine.

At the same time, some participants and their supporters argue that channels of dialogue should remain open even during periods of heightened tensions.

Ukrainian sources have raised a different concern: if the discussions were about the war in Ukraine, why was Ukraine itself not represented at the table? That question remains unanswered, and any conclusions at this stage remain speculative.

Russia’s response

Moscow’s initial reaction was predictable and came in the form of a warning. Alexander Tolmachyov, a member of Russia’s State Duma, told Lenta.ru that Baku was “following Armenia’s path”, arguing that closer ties with Europe had brought neither Ukraine nor Armenia success.

That prompted a sharp response in an article published by Minval.az. The author argued that Azerbaijan had never accepted Moscow’s vision of a “big brother”, had chosen not to join the CSTO, and had consistently pursued a multi-vector foreign policy. In the author’s view, the strategic partnership with Germany does not represent “turning away from Russia” but rather reflects a pragmatic approach. Notably, Baku has framed the issue not in defensive terms but as its sovereign right to make its own decisions.

Other assessments have been more nuanced. German critics view the meetings in Baku as evidence of weaknesses in Berlin’s Russia policy and an attempt to revive old German-Russian political ties.

A different perspective emerges in analyses by the Kyiv Post and the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. They argue that while Baku continues to support Ukraine’s territorial integrity and expand cooperation with Kyiv, it has not completely severed channels of communication with Moscow, seeking instead to preserve room for diplomatic manoeuvre.

Taken together, the Berlin briefing suggested not so much a decisive “pivot to the West” as a policy of careful balancing. Azerbaijan’s energy interests are increasingly tied to Europe, its security calculations continue to take Russia into account, and its stated position remains grounded in support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity.

Call for investment in gas infrastructure

The second major theme of the Berlin briefing attracted less controversy but carried greater strategic significance. Aliyev announced that Azerbaijan had begun supplying natural gas to Germany this year. Under a ten-year contract, initial deliveries amount to around 1.5 billion cubic metres annually. However, he said any increase in volumes would depend on two factors: additional purchase commitments and expanded infrastructure.

According to Aliyev, both the TANAP and TAP pipelines are already operating at full capacity, leaving no spare transit capacity. Expanding infrastructure within Europe and building new interconnectors will therefore require additional investment. He singled out the European Investment Bank’s decision to stop financing oil and gas projects under the EU’s green transition policy as one of the key obstacles.

The ten-year gas supply agreement between SEFE and SOCAR reinforces this trend. In June, Germany’s ambassador to Azerbaijan, Ralf Horlemann, said contracts signed by German companies provide for annual imports of around 2 billion cubic metres of Azerbaijani gas.

The political message was clear: Baku is urging Europe to help finance the expansion of gas infrastructure. Merz likewise stressed that Germany has a strong interest in diversifying its gas imports.

The scope for increasing gas deliveries to Europe via the Southern Gas Corridor now depends less on political declarations than on whether European countries are willing to invest in new infrastructure. The contradiction is evident: Europe needs additional gas supplies to strengthen its energy security, yet remains reluctant to finance gas projects as part of its green transition agenda.

Declaration on a Strategic Partnership

The Joint Declaration on the Strategic Agenda of the Bilateral Partnership between the Republic of Azerbaijan and the Federal Republic of Germany, signed on 21 July, is a wide-ranging document drafted in technical language.

It outlines cooperation across a broad spectrum of areas, including high-level political dialogue and diplomatic consultations; the German-Azerbaijani High-Level Working Group on Trade and Investment; energy cooperation, including natural gas supplies; renewable energy; low-carbon hydrogen; energy efficiency; transport connectivity and infrastructure; security and defence; humanitarian demining; as well as culture, education, science and innovation.

The declaration also reaffirms Germany’s support for the normalisation of relations between Azerbaijan and Armenia and for peace initiatives launched after the Washington summit on 8 August 2025. It further highlights the “strategic importance” of the partnership between Azerbaijan and the European Union.

What does it mean?

First, the agreement formally elevates relations between Azerbaijan and Germany to the level of a strategic partnership.

Second, Baku is signalling that its cooperation with Germany extends well beyond natural gas. The agenda also includes renewable energy, transport and logistics, industrial modernisation, science and innovation.

Third, Berlin appears to be viewing the South Caucasus not only through the lens of values and norms, but increasingly in terms of energy security and transport connectivity.

In other words, the declaration is more than a symbolic political statement. It provides a framework for expanding German-Azerbaijani cooperation and institutionalising the European dimension of Azerbaijan’s foreign policy.

Ilham Aliyev’s Berlin briefing

World.title: Oil prices jump back over $US100 a barrel as Middle East conflict widens
World.content:
Oil prices have tipped back over $US100 a barrel ($143) for the first time in two months, as the US president vows to hold Iran responsible for any attacks by the Houthi rebels in Yemen on Saudi oil tankers.

The Houthis announced a blockade of long-time enemies Saudi Arabia earlier in the week, following a flare up in their more then decade long war.

It has led to disruptions to shipping in the Red Sea, and specifically through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait between Yemen and the Horn of Africa.

In a post on his Truth Social platform, US President Donald Trump said the Houthis had opened fire on two Saudi tankers on Wednesday.

"Please let this TRUTH serve to represent that if they do this again, the U.S. will hold Iran responsible, in that the Houthis are a Surrogate and/or Proxy of Iran, and major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis, themselves, who I am very disappointed with in that they have, until now, acted very professionally and smart," he said.

The Houthis announced a blockade of a vital Saudi shipping route. (Reuters: Khaled Abdullah)

Iranian state media later reported sounds of explosions on Qeshm Island, located in the Strait of Hormuz.

The president also cited previous US strikes on the Houthis in his post.

"A year ago the United States of America attacked, very powerfully, the Houthis, for their interference with commerce and trade, by shooting at ships," he posted.

The Saudis had been using the Bab el-Mandeb, which translates to "Gate of Tears" to ship oil otherwise blocked from global markets by Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz, on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula.

The US 'signal' hidden in a nuclear deal Analysts warn the US and Saudi Arabia's landmark deal could set off a "nuclear arms race in the Middle East".

The oil-rich nation pumped millions of barrels through its East-West pipeline, taking supplies from its large east coast production hubs to its Yanbu port on the west coast.

Both the pipeline and the Yanbu facility were attacked by Iran at the height of the US and Israel's war against Tehran.

Brent Crude rose more than 6 per cent on Thursday, crashing through the $US100 a barrel price, off the back of the blockade concerns.

Earlier, the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters at the ASEAN summit in the Philippines he believed the Houthis had been "suckered into" the war by their Iranian backers.

The Reuters news agency has reported the Saudi state-owned oil company Aramco has begun offering customers more oil shipments from ports in Egypt, as it seeks to avoid the Houthi blockade.

US President Donald Trump is issuing another threat to Iran, this time warning that he will hold the country responsible for Houthi attacks. (Reuters: Saul Loeb)

Both sides launch attacks

The development comes as the Middle East region remains on high alert, with daily fire between the US and Iran across the Persian Gulf and beyond.

The US has continued to attack Iranian infrastructure along the gulf coast, following Mr Trump's warning that bridges and power stations would be targeted if the Iranians attacked ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

In response, Iran continued to launch missiles and drones at claimed US military targets in the region, including sites in Jordan.

The Jordanian army said Iran fired four missiles and six drones at the kingdom, triggering the country's air defence systems.

It's now more than a fortnight since Donald Trump declared the interim deal he signed with Iran to immediately end fighting, and begin negotiations on the future of its nuclear program and the management of the Strait of Hormuz, was over.

The war with Iran is now almost five months old.

To this point, Israel has not returned to the fighting, however authorities have been monitoring the deteriorating situation closely.

Local media has reported some municipalities have reopened public bomb shelters ahead of any strike by the Iranians on Israel, although the Israeli military's Home Front Command has not issued any formal directive at this point.

Some hospitals were reportedly also preparing their fortified underground wards.

World.title: Saudi Arabia must recognise Israel for nuclear deal, says Trump
World.content:
Donald Trump is insisting the US deal allowing Saudi Arabia to develop a nuclear energy industry has one major condition — the Arab kingdom must formally recognise the State of Israel.

In his first comments about the nuclear agreement since its announcement, President Trump said Saudi Arabia would have to join the Abraham Accords for the deal to go ahead, and also said there would be no enrichment of uranium by Riyadh under the plan.

The US has long seen the normalisation of ties between Saudi Arabia and Israel as one of its great diplomatic goals, given the power and influence the oil-rich nation has in the region.

The Biden administration seemed to come close to achieving that, before the war in Gaza erupted and Saudi Arabia took a far harder stance against Israel.

It has previously said it would only recognise Israel if Israel in turn recognised a Palestinian state — something the Netanyahu Government has refused to do.

"The Civil Nuclear Deal (There will be no enrichment of material!) being made between the United States Department of Energy and Saudi Arabia, which pertains only to non-military use such as the ones that Iran and UAE (and others) already have, will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords," President Trump posted on his Truth Social platform.

The deal between Washington and Riyadh was announced by press release on Wednesday in the US, with many of its terms kept tightly under wraps, and there was no mention of the Abraham Accords in the scant detail which was released.

White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt effectively confirmed the Abraham Accords condition was added after the announcement of the deal, and said President Trump had not spoken to Saudi Arabia's de facto leader Mohammed bin Salman about the issue.

She said it should not be a surprise, given his recent comments on the matter.

The original announcement had fuelled anger in Israel, which immediately saw the deal as having the potential to fuel a race to secure nuclear weapons across the Middle East — even though the agreement is focused on nuclear energy.

US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. (File photo via Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

Israel has its own highly secretive nuclear industry, although it has not publicly acknowledged having nuclear weapons.

Opposition politicians Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman led the criticism of the deal on Wednesday, saying it opened the door to Saudi Arabia developing nuclear weapons and enriching uranium.

Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office leapt on the suggestion from the US President.

"The joint American and Israeli military action against the genocidal regime in Tehran and Israel's crushing of Iran's terror axis have created the possibility to expand the circle of peace,” it said in a statement

"As President Trump has said, Saudi Arabia's joining of the Abraham Accords would be an historic leap forward for peace in the Middle East.

“Peace through strength."

Saudi Arabia has been racing to diversify its economy, and its own energy supplies, using massive amounts of its oil-wealth to fund the transformation.

The US President has strengthened ties with the kingdom while in office, spruiking his personal relationship with Mohammed bin Salman.

The Crown Prince has used his influence with President Trump in recent years, including working with Turkiye's President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan to convince the White House to drop crippling sanctions on Syria following the fall of the Assad regime.

Mohammed bin Salman has previously said that if Iran developed a nuclear weapon, Saudi Arabia would follow.

President Trump previously floated the idea of Arab nations joining the Abraham Accords as part of any deal to end the war with Iran - but signed the interim ceasefire anyway, despite no countries signing up.

That deal has since fallen over, with a return to daily strikes across the Persian Gulf and beyond into Jordan.

World.title: Billions in new funding for AUKUS shipyards in Adelaide
World.content:
The shipyards that will construct Australia's fleet of AUKUS nuclear-powered submarines have been handed a $4.6 billion funding boost.

The additional investment will help further develop the new Submarine Construction Yard at Adelaide's Osborne shipyards.

The announcement, to be made on Friday, comes on the sidelines of the ALP's 50th National Conference in Adelaide which appears set to avoid a public debate over the AUKUS pact.

Billions of dollars in state and federal funding are going into the shipyards to prepare for the submarine construction project, with the first AUKUS-class submarine to be delivered in the early 2040s.

This funding boost comes on top of $3.9 billion already announced for the commonwealth Australian Naval Infrastructure shipyards earlier this year.

Two AUKUS submarine optimal pathways Scrutiny of AUKUS's delivery reveals two "optimal pathways" for Australia's submarines.

Australian Naval Infrastructure is a commonwealth-owned company.

Under AUKUS, five nuclear-powered submarines will be constructed at Osborne, on top of the three Virginia-class submarines being acquired from the United States.

Construction on Australia's fleet of Hunter Class frigates is already underway, but the new submarine shipyards are expected to be 10 times the size of the existing precinct.

The development includes the construction of a 420-metre-long fabrication hall, along with outfitting, consolidating and commissioning precincts within the yard.

The government is seeking to highlight the jobs that will be created during construction, with 1,100 people already employed on the site and thousands more expected in South Australia.

Peter Malinauskas has highlighted the scale of the project. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said the funding was another step on the path towards making the AUKUS nuclear-powered submarine program a reality.

"This investment is another important step in building the sovereign capability Australia will need to build, operate, maintain and sustain our future submarine fleet," he said.

"The work underway right now at Osborne demonstrates that AUKUS is on track and happening now, all while creating opportunities for Australian industry and workers for decades to come."

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas said it was an enormous undertaking.

"It is difficult to comprehend the scale of the billions of dollars of investment being delivered at Osborne to enable us to build the most complex machines on the planet," he said.

Construction underway across the country

This funding announcement brings the total volume invested into the Osborne shipyards under AUKUS to $8.5 billion in taxpayer funds.

But that funding is still dwarfed by other AUKUS projects, including the $12 billion announced for the Henderson shipyards in Western Australia last year.

Henderson will maintain the Virginia Class submarines Australia will operate from the 2030s, along with AUKUS submarines.

This new multi-billion-dollar funding announcement comes as Labor's national conference takes place in Adelaide.

Australia is expected to operate the US Navy's Virginia-class submarines from the 2030s. (Supplied: US Department of Defense)

While AUKUS was publicly debated at Labor's last national conference three years ago, it appears unlikely to flare up at this year's conference.

Despite some concerns over the pact within parts of Labor's rank-and-file membership, and Labor MP Ed Husic calling for the pact to be renegotiated, the conference appears to be set to avoid another public discussion of AUKUS.

That has caused dismay among some of the pact's most vocal opponents, like former Labor minister Peter Garrett, who is leading a "public inquiry" into AUKUS at present.

"This week's Labor conference in Adelaide — one of the key locations for AUKUS, as it happens — looks unlikely to accommodate any meaningful debate on the issue," he said in a piece for Guardian Australia.

"This is a great pity."

World.title: Netball agents frustrated as pay talks roll into Glasgow 2026
World.content:
Has netball learned much since 2023? You be the judge.

The messy and drawn-out pay negotiations that dominated headlines during that World Cup year are once again overshadowing a major tournament for the sport.

The Diamonds are aiming to defend gold at the Commonwealth Games, and that mission starts on Saturday night in their opening match against Tonga at 8pm AEST. But the world number one team hit the court in Glasgow with uncertain futures.

The current Super Netball collective player agreement (CPA) expires on September 30, meaning all 88 players will be off contract. It is a chaotic way of doing things and leads to a mad scramble for everyone involved, with so many trying to secure opportunity at the same time.

Netball Australia surrenders, as players win long and bitter pay war Netball Australia has finally agreed to a modest revenue share partnership with its players, but how much have its brutal tactics throughout the pay negotiations damaged the game?

The 2027 signing window was supposed to open the Monday after the grand final on July 4. That has been delayed a month so the athletes can focus on their international duties while the terms of the next deal are worked through.

There are several sticking points that the national sporting organisation and the Australian Netball Players' Association (ANPA) cannot agree on. More on that later.

It is important to note that ANPA provided a detailed submission late last year to try and get the ball rolling. Netball Australia wanted to wait and sort out its new broadcast agreement with Nine, which underwrites the majority of the costs of the CPA first. That was done in April.

Although from the sport's point of view, discussions are more respectful and constructive this time, with greater transparency of information shared amongst parties, the players are incredibly frustrated. And so are their agents, who argue they are unable to make meaningful progress on behalf of their talent.

There is no prohibition to hold non-binding conversations with your own club or another right now, yet a request to allow non-binding written offers while CPA talks take place was denied. The agents believe this would've freed up the system and given players more certainty.

Kathryn Deiulioi is the founder of Behind Your Brand, which manages several Diamonds athletes, including the Australian captain. (Image Supplied)

Kathryn Deiulio, the founder of Behind Your Brand, said it was her understanding that the Diamonds players did not ask the sport to push back the contracting window and wanted discussions to continue. There are concerns this kind of assumption could create a divide amongst the group, positioning some as more important than others.

"This misunderstanding creates the impression that they didn't consider the impact it could have on the remaining 60-70 players not playing at the Games," Deiulio told ABC Sport.

"It is our role to continue contract negotiations on their behalf, and it would have created an additional layer of complexity, given the time difference and the need to carefully manage communication with players so as not to distract them from their performance.

"However, ultimately, that is part of our role as agents and something we are equipped to manage … These are professional athletes who dedicate their lives to their sport, and they deserve the same level of security around employment expected in any other profession."

Australia won gold at the Commonwealth Games in Birmingham. (Getty: Sue McKay)

Jace Bode is the chief executive of W Sports & Media, which works across a range of elite codes, such as cricket, Aussie Rules, football, golf and tennis.

"The fact that 80-plus athletes have once again been put in this position is incredibly disappointing and challenging to manage from our perspective," Bode told ABC Sport.

"We have the best netball competition in the world, and it is frustrating to watch these athletes continue to navigate uncertainty around their careers when it has so much potential."

This CPA will only be a 12-month deal, allowing Netball Australia to try and bring in more revenue from 2027 onwards with the free-to-air broadcast agreement and present a stronger offer. But both agents worry that without a longer CPA in place we may be right back here next year, ahead of a World Cup on home soil.

The Diamonds players have been in camp since Friday July 10. (Supplied: Netball Australia)

According to the new dates, contracts will open for clubs' own players from August 4-16. Non-binding written offers are permitted for all players during these 12 days. Then, from August 17-28, contracting officially opens for those looking to switch allegiances.

The agents argue this process favours those who intend to remain at their existing club, while placing players who may be looking elsewhere at a significant disadvantage. The time frame is also not ideal for those weighing up their options overseas, with the English Superleague contracting window already in full swing.

Complicating things further, in other sports it is normally the responsibility of the governing body to handle CPA talks with the players' association, but here the clubs appear to have taken greater control of the wheel.

All eight Super Netball franchises are likely to have competing ideas slowing progress further, and it is unclear if their vested interests will be prioritised over what is best for the sport as a whole.

Shimona Nelson represents Jamaica at the Birmingham Commonwealth Games. (Getty: Mark Kolbe)

The delay has wide-reaching implications beyond the Australian team at the Games.

In-form Melbourne Mavericks star Shimona Nelson had already flagged with Netball Jamaica that she would be unavailable for selection for Glasgow ahead of the Super Netball season. The goal shooter needs to get her tonsils removed and deal with a knee issue.

Although the Sunshine Girls did try and get her to change her mind, an appearance at the major tournament would be risky. Should she injure herself, with only one-year contracts being offered, where would that leave her?

It makes sense that Nelson has put herself first, considering the history of her career. After the Collingwood team disbanded, Nelson had to forge her way back into the league as a No.11 player with the Mavericks, working hard to return to a full-time contract the next season.

It is unfair that athletes are being forced to make these tricky decisions based on what is happening in Super Netball, and what is right for each of them is extremely individual.

Shimona Jok keeping an open mind as 11th player signing confirms she's eligible for Diamonds Super Netball import Shimona Jok was in the headlines after the Mavericks found a loophole to sign her as their 11th player. But now her eligibility for the Diamonds has been confirmed, would she ever go there?

There has been a rumour that Nelson isn't playing because she instead wants to represent the Diamonds at the next World Cup.

Nelson indeed plans to get her citizenship in September, purely to cement her status in a country she has lived in for almost 10 years and now classes as home.

At this point, there have been no discussions between the Australian camp or Shimona's about the possibility of her playing for the Diamonds.

So, what are some of the sticking points of the CPA talks?

Currently on the table is a 25 per cent pay increase for those on the minimum wage and a three per cent pay increase for everyone else.

This all sounds rosy until you do the numbers. Australia's consumer price index sits at four per cent. Once these changes are factored into the salary cap, with increased superannuation contributions and the rising cost of living, the take-home pay for many of the athletes could actually be worse off than they were this year. It may lead to a pay cut in real terms.

Former Thunderbird and Diamond Kathryn Harby-Williams is the chief executive of the players' association. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

Despite this, the sport will continue to restrict player opportunities to make extra cash in sponsorship deals. The cap for commercial arrangements with an existing team sponsor or partner is going to be raised to $50,000 but the agents want the cap removed entirely.

There are no monetary limits on a player's commercial agreements with third parties, but agents find the amount of compliance their talent must go through to get approval is unreasonable and leads to sponsors turning to athletes from other codes.

"When athletes are able to work with brands and authentically leverage their own platforms, they bring different eyeballs to the sport … This should be viewed as a positive, not a threat," Bode and Deiulio said.

"If netball does not evolve in this increasingly competitive female sports landscape, these limitations will have a broader impact on its growth and visibility."

World.title: Death toll climbs after flooding in India, Afghanistan and Pakistan
World.content:
At least 82 people have died in 72 hours after heavy rain and flash flooding began sweeping through India, Pakistan and Afghanistan.

More than 650,000 people have been affected across 11 districts in the Indian state of Assam, according to the state's disaster management authority.

Local authorities said at least 10 people had died in the past 24 hours, taking the death toll in India to 36.

At least 46 people have been killed and more than 100 people injured across Afghanistan and Pakistan, according to disaster management authorities in both countries.

The extent of damage in some parts of Afghanistan is undetermined. (AP Photo: Wahidullah Kakar)

The Nuristan governor's office confirmed one of the district mayors, Sayed Ahmad Arhabi, had died in the floods.

Infrastructure damage

The Afghanistan National Disaster Management Authority said the water had caused an undetermined number of buildings to collapse.

The provincial capital city of Parun, in India, was among the areas affected, authorities said.

Flooded roads meant cars and machinery were unable to navigate parts of Lahore, which flooded in recent heavy rain in Pakistan. (AP Photo: K.M Chaudary)

Farid Gul Zaheer, a pharmacist in the region, said he had "never witnessed such a dangerous flood".

"It felt like there was an earthquake, and I heard children and people screaming,

"Everyone is traumatised, they didn't sleep all night," Mr Zaheer said.

Mr Zaheer said he had "lost everything".

It comes after widespread flooding and landslides killed 110 people in Afghanistan earlier this year.

Search difficulties

Flooding began earlier in the week after heavy rainfall between July 18 and 20, resulting in unusually high river flows.

Rescue searches in Afghanistan were underway on Tuesday when two gunshots were heard, a signal that more flooding was imminent.

Residents and rescue workers inspect buildings damaged by heavy flooding in Nuristan, Afghanistan. (AP Photo: Wahidullah Kakar)

Juma Khan Nayel, communications chief for the Afghan Red Crescent Society, said the water rose to unprecedented levels.

Afghanistan's defence ministry said the military had also been deployed to the area to support the relief effort, while the United Nations said it was assessing the disaster.

World.title: Chinese diplomats leave ALP conference after bid to eject Taiwan officials
World.content:
Chinese diplomats left Labor's national conference after complaining to ALP National Secretary Paul Erickson about the presence of Taiwanese officials at the high-profile political gathering in Adelaide.

Three Chinese diplomats observing the conference confronted Mr Erickson on Thursday morning to demand that two representatives from Taiwan's de facto embassy in Canberra — the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Australia — be ejected from the venue.

The incident was first reported by The Australian on Thursday.

The ALP has confirmed that Mr Erickson then made it clear that the TECO representatives were entitled to attend as observers, and would be allowed to remain.

Anthony Albanese addresses the 50th National Labor Conference in Adelaide. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

China effectively stages walk-out in protest, source tells ABC

Multiple sources told the ABC that the Chinese delegation left the venue in the hours after the exchange, and did not join other foreign diplomats and political representatives watching the conference that afternoon.

It is not yet clear whether their departure was intended as a deliberate protest — although other diplomatic observers at the conference told the ABC that it was hard to interpret it in any other way.

One Labor delegate also told the ABC that it was "obvious" that China had effectively staged a walk-out.

"They lodge a protest and then they leave — it's clearly a signal," they said.

The ABC has asked the Chinese Embassy in Canberra why its diplomats left the venue, but it has not yet responded.

Incident could ignite new tension

An ALP spokesperson declined to say if the delegation gave a reason for their departure, saying it was a question for the Chinese Embassy.

The incident could stir fresh tensions between China and Australia in the wake of several recent high profile disputes — including over Beijing's missile test in the Pacific, confrontations between China and the Philippines in the South China Sea, and Australia's new strategic pacts with both Fiji and Vanuatu.

China, Philippines clash in South China Sea Vision posted online by the Philippines Coast Guard shows Filipino and Chinese personnel briefly engaging each other from inflatable boats, with the Philippines accusing China of assaulting one of its navy staff.

The two representatives from Taiwan's office are attending as general observers rather than as "international observers" — which includes foreign diplomats and representatives of political parties from multiple countries.

But China has been taking an increasingly hard line on Taiwan as it tries to diplomatically isolate the democratically ruled island, and has been ramping up pressure on countries across the globe to cut or downgrade even unofficial ties with Taipei.

Last week, China heaped praise on Papua New Guinea after it announced that it would shut down Taipei's representative office in Port Moresby.

Political parties allowed to have Taiwanese observers in attendance, Chinese expert says

Mark Harrison, who is a senior lecturer in Chinese Studies at the University of Tasmania, told the ABC that nothing in Australia's One China policy — which acknowledges Beijing's claim over Taiwan without endorsing it — prevented political parties like the ALP from allowing Taiwanese observers to attend.

"Our One China policy applies to the national government — a political party is not bound by it," he said.

"If a political party wants to give an opportunity for an external group to observe then it's entirely appropriate to do so.

"And given the deep trade complementarity (between Australia and Taiwan) it's entirely appropriate for these opportunities to be offered and taken advantage of."

China demands Australia stop 'inciting confrontation' over South China Sea China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs has demanded Australia stop "exaggerating tensions and inciting confrontation" over the South China Sea after Penny Wong warned Beijing against "destabilising" conduct in the region.

Dr Harrison also praised Mr Erickson's response to the pressure from China, saying it was "an appropriate response to the effort by the Chinese side" to shape Labor's decisions.

"It's important from the Australian side that government and other organisations subject to that effort understand the importance of setting clear boundaries," he said.

The ABC has asked the foreign minister's office whether China has lodged any official diplomatic protests with Australia over the incident.

World.title: SA police say man dies while resisting arrest in Adelaide CBD
World.content:
A man has died in the Adelaide CBD after police say he became unresponsive during an attempted arrest this afternoon.

Police were called to West Terrace just after 4:15pm, following reports a man was behaving in a disorderly manner and damaging vehicles.

Police said they attempted to arrest the man, but he resisted and became unresponsive.

In a statement, SA Police said, "Despite the efforts of police and paramedics who performed CPR, he died at the scene."

A report is being prepared for the state coroner, and the death will be subject to a Police Commissioner's Inquiry.

World.title: Australia gets first win with Glasgow asleep and the Games yet to open
World.content:
In a world where everything costs a bit too much and "free summer holiday activities" is high in your auto-complete drop-down, a spot of barefoot bowls remains a glorious tradition.

The sun shining, warming your carbonated beverage to a few degrees warmer than is pleasant, baffling yourself with how you can be so bad at a sport that on its face seems so simple, all while trying to stay alive to the prospect of your mates accidentally breaking your toe with wildly flung rock while misquoting half-remembered lines from Crackerjack.

That wasn't quite the case as the sport kicked off the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

How we got to Glasgow 2026 The bumpy road to Glasgow 2026 has produced a Commonwealth Games that will look a little different than the ones that came before.

The city of Glasgow was still waking up as athletes, officials and a handful of fans filed into the Scottish Event Campus (SEC) for a 9:30am start to Commonwealth competition on Thursday.

Not least of which because the event isn't on lawn of any sort; it's being played on carpeted greens indoors at the SEC Centre.

It serves as a reminder of organisers' decision to hold as many events in existing halls and venues, and gives the in-house DJ prime acoustics as he tries to pump up a crowd described as "small but mighty" by the MC team.

Already the only sport running on every day of the Games, organisers added an extra session on Day Zero before the opening ceremony due to "unprecedented demand" for the sport at a distinctly Scottish Games.

The sport has the royal seal of approval. (Getty Images: Aaron Chown/WPA Pool)

But making that widely known to punters may have fallen by the wayside for an organising committee feeling the pinch as their rapid 22-month planning period suddenly reached its end.

Along with bowls, the SEC will host more than half – boxing, judo, 3x3 basketball, netball, weightlifting and para powerlifting – of the cut-down list of sports in Glasgow.

Everything from Naughty By Nature to drum and pipes renditions of ABBA and Tina Turner echoed through Hall 3 as the countdown began and pyrotechnics welcomed the athletes to the rinks, with Australia's 2018 gold medallist Kelsey Cottrell the consensus "one to watch" as eight women's pairs rollers and four in the men's singles stepped onto the field of play.

But the first competitive moments of Glasgow 2026 arrived with a startling lack of fanfare, at least for the uninitiated.

There was fanfare welcoming the first Commonwealth Games athletes to the arena. (Bowls Australia: Aidan Davis)

The in-arena announcer made sure to point out their warm-up rolls had no bearing on the scores, but the only marker that Jackaroos Cottrell and Dawn Hayman were officially kicking us off came when the scoreboard clicked on at the far end of the Siti Zalina Ahmad Rink.

Cottrell and Hayman got it ticking over straight away with a 4-0 lead after the first end of the first set against Gertrude Siame and Foster Banda.

It was the sort of lead you see sometimes at these sorts of meets, where one team is simply outclassed.

That was certainly happening in the concurrent men's singles, where 39-year-old former world champion Shannon McIlroy was kicking the tar out of 17-year-old Tongan Liam Hill, and Northern Ireland's Gary Kelly was rolling Frederrick Tafatu of Niue.

The biggest cheers of the morning came from Botswana's crew whenever bucket-hatted Diza Mphotho won an end, a raucous reaction that cracked through the polite hum and mild applause accompanying some of the other victories.

Meanwhile, the Zambian pair fought back before Cottrell got the Aussie team rocking on the sidelines with a clutch final roll to secure the 6-4 win in the first set.

A vocal Zambian team gave the Aussies a scare. (Bowls Australia: Aidan Davis)

"Just breathe through the nerves a little bit when you feel that adrenaline pumping on the mat," Cottrell said.

"Take that extra second; time is precious [with a 30-second shot clock], but take that extra second and breathe through it."

The heavily favoured Aussies looked more like themselves in the second set as they romped to a 2-0 win against a team that had never played on carpet before.

Even as they were getting walloped 14-0 in the second set, Zambian skip Banda was vocally gassing up her partner – "Come on Gertrude, you are trying my darling" – and apologising for her own performances.

It was a welcome distraction for the Australians as they tried to keep their own adrenaline in check.

"They're always very chatty," Cottrell said.

"It's just that fine line, being able to walk away and focus when we need to, but also it's kind of good to engage in it because it keeps us cool, calm and collected as well. Really lovely girls."

Hayman and Cottrell will walk in the opening ceremony at the Hydro from 5am on Friday (AEST), but they have already truly opened the 2026 Commonwealth Games.

World.title: Perth’s cheapest petrol chain hauls landlords to court over eviction notices
World.content:
NationalWACourts Perth’s cheapest petrol chain hauls landlords to court over eviction notices Hannah Murphy July 24, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Perth’s cheapest petrol station chain is suing its landlords, alleging they tried to kick the business out of five sites around the state. Burk Fuel has lodged a writ in WA’s Supreme Court against five corporate entities who leased sites to the cheap fuel carrier, alleging in one instance the landlord swooped into one of its petrol stations in Arthur River in May and terminated its lease. Burk Fuel have 15 locations around the state. Burk Fuel Burk Fuel was registered as a business in 2021 and has slowly expanded across the state, often undercutting its nearest competitors by anywhere between 15 and 30 cents on the litre. The company alleged one of the landlords “failed in accordance with the lease for the Arthur River site to rectify structural damage to the building … and without notice entered possession of and thereby terminated the lease for the Arthur River site”.



The writ went on to claim Burk was a lessor another four sites across WA, including in Williams, Carabbin, Camillo and Beaufort River, all leased by different corporate entities based out of the same address in Melbourne. Related Article Updated

Petrol prices Bowser bungle sees Cannington servo sell WA’s most expensive diesel and cheapest unleaded About two months after the landlord took back the Arthur River site, the writ claimed, it also came knocking for four of its other leases – including in Williams, Carrabin, Camillo and Beaufort River. Burk Fuel was handed a notice to forfeit and terminate the leases. In the writ, published in the Supreme Court this week, Burk alleged the evictions represented a breach of all four separate leases, and called for damages over the forfeiture and termination of the leases.



“[The plaintiff claims] special damages, including loss of business, loss of profits, loss of goodwill, relocation costs and other losses suffered by the plaintiff because of the conduct of [the defendants],” the writ said. At this stage, Burk remains at the four sites, but has closed the site at Arthur River. In the writ, Burk said it intended to fight the evictions at the remaining four sties. The five sites make up about one third of Burk’s total outlets across WA and in Victoria. The Supreme Court action is not the first time the petrol company fought out contracts with its suppliers and stakeholders via the legal system. Just three years after Burk, operated by brothers Umar Farooq and Haris Farooq, began at its first site in Alkimos, it was hauled before the Supreme Court by a fuel transportation company for an alleged breach of contract.



The company is currently under investigation by authorities for its fuel quality. Burk Fuel Paramount Haulage sued the Farooqs after they made a 10-year exclusive fuel transportation agreement with the company, meaning all fuel transport had to be done by Paramount Haulage trucks. The deal was due to start in May 2022, and run until May 2032. However, Paramount Haulage alleged Burk soon decided to end the agreement and begin running fuel with their own trucks. In its defence, Burk alleged Paramount had told them they were set for price increases, and either the company agreed to an increase operating cost, or accept Paramount may need to sell its trucks and exit the fuel transportation business altogether. The matter was eventually settled out of court.



Burk Fuel’s petrol quality is also currently under investigation by Consumer Protection, after Business News revealed samples taken from the bowsers of four Burk fuel stations in September 2025 alleged Burk was selling Premium 95 fuel that was consistent with 91. The investigation is due to hand down its findings in September.

World.title: ‘Says more about the crowd than it does about Isaac’: Pendlebury speaks out on Crows fans booing Quaynor
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Says more about the crowd than it does about Isaac’: Pendlebury speaks out on Crows fans booing Quaynor Steve Barrett July 24, 2026 — 12:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Adelaide: Collingwood champion Scott Pendlebury says the Adelaide Oval crowd’s booing of Isaac Quaynor on Thursday night says more about those fans than it does about his teammate. Playing his 150th game, Quaynor was jeered by large sections of the 50,109-strong crowd for every one of his 20 disposals as the Magpies turned a 27-point first-half deficit into a powerful 34-point win over Adelaide. Isaac Quaynor was again subjected to boos at Adelaide Oval. AFL Photos Quaynor was also targeted by Crows supporters in last year’s qualifying final, a fortnight after he was the victim of a homophobic slur from Adelaide star Izak Rankine. “I definitely noticed it at the start of the game,” said Pendlebury, who racked up 29 disposals, six clearances and kicked a momentum-turning goal late in the second quarter.



“It probably says more about the crowd than it does about Isaac. “Stuff happens in footy all the time, but I think as supporters from all sides, and the league in general, we’ve just got to be better.” Nick Daicos was at his awe-inspiring best yet again against the Crows. AFL Photos Pendlebury doesn’t believe Quaynor was rattled by the hostile reception, but said he and his fellow Magpies will rally around the gun backman regardless. “He’ll be fine,” Pendlebury said.



“Isaac probably knew it was going to come. We’re all big boys and we’ll get around Isaac, but he’ll be fine.” Related Article AFL 2026 The Craig McRae coaching masterclass that inspired a stunning Magpies comeback victory Victorious Collingwood coach Craig McRae brought his daughter Charlie to the post-match press conference. He used the opportunity to speak about the values he has instilled in his family around not booing sportspeople while questioning why Quaynor was being treated as though he had done something wrong. “I’ve got my little daughter in the room – she’s 10,” McRae said. “I teach her [that] we don’t boo. That’s all I can control.



“It’s a fascinating narrative around why they would boo him. “My understanding is he was the victim of a homophobic slur, and he’s getting booed for that? It’s a fascinating world we live in.” View post on X While unhappy with the behaviour of those fans, McRae also made it clear he held no ill will towards Rankine, who he sought out after the final siren. “I actually grabbed Izak Rankine at the end of the game and said, ‘We’ve got great respect for you, young man’,” McRae revealed.



“People are allowed to make mistakes – they are. We’re all human. View post on X “We’ve got great respect for him – he’s a sensational player. “I don’t know him as a person, but the way he stood up and overcame what was – [he] took it on the shoulders – there’s something to be said about that. “That’s life, isn’t it? Make a mistake, fix it and improve yourself.



View post on X “We were rapt in our Isaac’s game tonight. Jeez, he must have had the ball a lot early because he got booed a lot. “We’ll get our arms around him [Quaynor] and show how much we love him.” Loading Adelaide coach Matthew Nicks during the week implored Crows fans to treat Quaynor with respect. His call to arms fell on deaf ears.



“The game’s a passionate game and sometimes we lose our way in that a little,” Nicks said. “With the backdrop and the background leading into this game, it’s not ideal the way it played out tonight.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Brisbane’s best cafes & bakeries (on the north side) in 2026
World.content:
Eating outFood Brisbane’s best cafes & bakeries (on the north side) in 2026 Our city’s cafes aren’t what they used to be. They’re better. From internationally known CBD coffee spots to expansive suburban cafes, here’s what you need to tick off. Matt Shea July 23, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What a difference a decade makes – particularly with a pandemic tossed in the middle. Brisbane’s cafe scene used to be dominated by full-service venues – places with a broad menu and a traditional ordering system. But COVID changed the game. These days it’s more about doing one or two things and doing them well, whether it’s coffee, sandwiches, baked goods or matcha. Don’t get us wrong: there are still great cafes in the traditional sense, but we’re living in the age of hyper-specialised venues, fancy bakeries and chef-run sandwich shops. But that just makes the AM dining and drinking scene all the more interesting. It also makes it harder to parse what’s worth your attention. Because in 2026 the tiniest coffee window could easily be making the best coffee.



So instead of rounding up the 60 best cafes in Brisbane, we’ve split it in two. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Next week, it will be everything south of the river. But this week, here are the 30 essential cafes, coffee spots, bakeries and sandwich shops in Brisbane’s north. Coffee Anthology and Fika Adam Wang’s Coffee Anthology is the yardstick by which all other

specialty coffee in this city is judged. Outside the Charlotte Street venue. Markus Ravik



Last year, it was ranked the eighth-best coffee shop in the world. Why? Because Wang presents the best roasters from around the country across espresso, filter and batch brew, with few compromises on technique or equipment. Since moving to Charlotte Street in 2022 it’s become part of the Intersection precinct, which also includes Fika, a slick full-service cafe that serves an elevated

Asian-inflected brunch. Good to know: Wang’s superb tilt at a roastery cafe, The Maillard Project, is located a few doors down the road. 155 Charlotte Street, Brisbane, intersectionfd.com.au Kin You know Kin. It’s the one with the coffee window beneath the heritage-

listed Australian Estates Woolstore building that draws Teneriffe’s bright

young things every morning, waiting patiently for their takeaway

Almanac coffee.



Kin serves elevated breakfasts in a beautiful dining room beneath a heritage-listed woolstore. But you need to sit down in Kin to truly understand its virtues: it’s in the brief but brilliant menu (dippy eggs with 24-month aged Valserena parmigiano reggiano, say, or a pad kra pao jaffle with makrut lime mayonnaise), the beautiful, homey dining room with its warm timber furnishings, and owners Tim and Allison MacIntyre’s hospitality, which is precise but genuine. A modern Brisbane classic. Good to know: Kin’s also a go-to for some of the best matcha in town. 24 Macquarie Street, Teneriffe, bykinbne.com Bellissimo



Australia’s most highly awarded coffee roaster hasn’t closed for a single

day since it opened in this Wandoo Street warehouse in January 2011. Outside Bellissimo Fortitude Valley. And more punters flock than ever before: for the exceptional specialty coffee, sure, but also a brunch menu that is perhaps better than it has any right to be. Bellissimo’s other outlets, in Coorparoo and Bulimba, are by now more well-rounded venues, but Wandoo Street remains the brand’s spiritual home. Good to know: Bellissimo’s breakfast burger is an unheralded contender for Brisbane’s best. 30 Wandoo Street, Fortitude Valley, bellissimocoffee.com.au





John Mills Himself All of Marcus Allison’s venues are worth your time: Anytime Coffee,

Bessa and Bunker Coffee. John Mills Himself can be found down an alleyway in the Brisbane CBD Michelle Smith But it’s John Mills Himself that makes this list on account of its unique digs (which, considering Bunker, is saying something) in an old print shop right in the guts of the city. That hidden setting, with its exposed brick, vintage lights and mosaic tile floor, will get the seekers through the door; the specialty coffee sourced from different roasters around the country does the rest. Good to know: The address is Charlotte Street but it’s easier to find via

Elizabeth – look for the laneway next to Thai on Time.



40 Charlotte Street, Brisbane, instagram.com/johnmillshimself Sprout Artisan Bakery One of Brisbane’s best bakeries is all grown up with this beautiful light-filled cafe on Skyring Terrace. Grab a seat inside. Morgan Roberts Also new is a short, sharp brunch menu that elegantly touches up the classics. What hasn’t changed is baker and co-owner Lutz Richter’s precisely folded and shaped seasonal fruit Danishes, berry croissant baskets, double chocolate croissant buns, cardamon custard scrolls and so much more. Espresso and specialty coffee comes via New Zealand’s Coffee Supreme.



Good to know: Yes, Richter and co-owner Rebecca Foley still maintain a presence at the Saturday Fresh Market in Rocklea. Shop 4/60 Skyring Terrace, Newstead, sproutartisanbakery.com.au Idle Agnes Bakery’s successor has everything that made it such a pandemic-era hit: the fire-licked sourdough loaves, Basque cheesecakes, caneles, kouign-amanns and so on – but also an all-day menu more imaginative than most around town, with daily salads and sandwiches added to the mix from 10am. Idle in New Farm. Markus Ravik



Coffee is by Sydney’s Single O and, of course, this is an Anyday venue so you know it looks a million dollars. Good to know: Part of the new(ish) Little Lane precinct, Idle’s neighbours include RUMA Rooftop, Green Cup and Johnny Gio Pizza. 84 Merthyr Road, New Farm, anyday.com.au/idle-venue-page Kosta’s Takeaway Benji Terkalas brought his viral, pandemic-era Sydney sandwich shop north in March, opening a tiny terracotta-tiled counter operation at Gasworks Plaza.



Schnitty sandwich. Morgan Roberts Onboard for its debut menu was star chef Adam Wolfers, whose influence shines in two sandwiches in particular: a chicken shawarma, and a breakfast yiros built with bifteki, egg and cheese. Otherwise, the breakfast and lunch menu covers sandwiches, toasties, focaccias, wraps and a pair of salads, with everything – other than the bread – made in-house. Coffee is by Canberra-based superstar

roaster Ona. Good to know: Yes, Kosta’s Instagrammable Schnitty sandwich is present and correct. 76 Skyring Terrace, Newstead, kostastakeaway.com Emme



Tommy Tze Lian’s restaurant that opened early has evolved into more of a breakfast cafe that finishes late. Emme on James Street. It’s in the morning that it absolutely heaves with customers, split between its handsome, stone-finished interior and a breezy dining island out front. But the care and precision of its woodfired dinner is reflected in breakfast dishes that include potatoes and eggs with cumin, fried garlic and chilli oil, and wagyu pastrami tartine with Russian sauce, pickles and a poached egg. A contender for

Brisbane’s best all-day dining spot right now. Good to know: Emme’s all-day dining means it serves it serves coffee to

the James Street massive until 3.30pm. Shop B03, 22 James Street, Fortitude Valley, emmejamesst.com



Baker D. Chirico Almost every weekend since its 2024 Brisbane debut, Melbourne-born

Baker D. Chirico has had queues out the door. Inside Baker D. Chirico’s Newstead outlet. Tammy Law Locals and interlopers come for the sourdough (made using a 25-year-old starter), bombolini and maritozzi, of course. But there’s also a greater focus here on savoury sandwiches, rolls and croissants. The shop itself is a striking evolution of the Carlton original’s “breadbasket” design, with a curved timber ceiling and reams of white terrazzo on the floors. Good to know: As of last week, Baker D. Chirico has (finally) started opening on Tuesdays.



18 Longland Street, Newstead, instagram.com/bakerdchirico Riser Bread Tom Cooney, Kieran Ryan and Duncan McKay opened Riser in 2022 in

the old Queenslander-style shopfront once occupied by the iconic

Bruno’s Tables, and more recently 85 Miskin Street. Riser is tucked away on a back street in bucolic Toowong. Morgan Roberts On weekends, it’s the scene of orderly chaos as customers compete for precisely baked Danishes, croissants, scrolls and sausage rolls, and a short selection of

fresh-made sandwiches that are among the best in town. For drinks, there’s Coffee Supreme coffee, hand-whisked matcha, craft sodas and fresh squeezed orange juice.



Good to know: It’s set up for grab-and-go but Riser’s upstairs courtyard

is one of the prettiest in town. 85 Miskin Street, Toowong, riserbread.com Bistro Tino Bistro Tino opened earlier this year in the old WWII-era Nissen hut premises previously occupied by King Arthur Cafe. Bistro Tino has opened in the premises previously occupied by King Arthur Cafe. Morgan Roberts



The Mosconi team has created a low-key stunner with beautiful parquetry, and mission brown and clothed cream colour palette. The food is just as good: think Italian sausage served with silverbeet, butter beans and baguette; or a potato and zucchini frittata served with blue swimmer crab and creme fraiche. For drinks, there’s Single O espresso, Somage teas and Hunted + Gathered organic hot chocolate. Good to know: Bistro Tino will begin opening for dinner in September. 164C Arthur Street, Fortitude Valley, instagram.com/bistro_tino Industry Beans



Opening in 2019, Industry Beans Newstead remains one of the city’s best

looking cafes, making the most of its light-filled warehouse space to

create the “breakfast restaurant” by which all others are measured. Indsutry Beans. The coffee menu is innovative and extensive, and the brunch menu has

improved to hit a sweet balance between approachable and elevated. It’s

not the most cutting-edge spot around but it remains a Northside brunch

date go-to for a reason. Good to know: This place sells stacks of beans and brewing equipment. 18 Proe Street, Newstead, industrybeans.com



Nodo Donuts Kate Williams’ Nodo was a game changer when it opened in Newstead in

2015 serving its baked-not-fried gluten-free doughnuts (they were

arguably more cake than doughnut, but the quality was exceptional, the

range of flavours imaginative). Nodo’s cake-like doughnuts remains as popular as ever. Must Do Brisbane Later, an expansion and a gluten-free brunch menu followed, as did other venues in the CBD and on the south side. It’s perhaps not as bleeding edge as it once was but those doughies remain undeniable. Good to know: Nodo has a stack of gluten-free flours and cake mixes

available in-store and online.



1 Ella Street, Newstead, nododonuts.com The Green Green by name, green by nature – a seat in this open-air stunner, among

its stacks of foliage, is a James Street prize on Saturday and Sunday

mornings. Moreish mezze in a sun-dappled courtyard at The Green. The Green The Middle Eastern menu is a cracker too: there’s Turkish eggs with muhammara, labne, hazelnut dukkha and house bread, crispy spiced garlic sujuk sausage, and Levant-spiced charcoal chicken. Coffee is by St. Ali.



Good to know: The Green goes late on Fridays and Saturdays. 1/27 James Street, Fortitude Valley, thegreen.com.au Yolk Yianni Pisarris took a “secret” menu item from his Morning After cafe in

West End and created a minor sensation when he opened Yolk at Gasworks in 2019. Yolk CBD. Dean Swindell



Its short menu was built around one thing: the perfect bacon and egg roll. Pisarris prefers a soft milk bun with streaky bacon, American cheese and a gooey fried egg. To that you can add your choice of sauce – including hollandaise, cayenne pepper hollandaise, chimichurri, and truffle mayo – and perhaps a hash brown (Pisarris reckons you should). Elsewhere on the menu there’s a steak and egg roll, a mushroom and egg roll, a chicken burger and a cheeseburger. Specialty coffee is by Five Senses. Good to know: Yolk opened a second store in the CBD (pictured here) earlier this year. 76 Skyring Terrace, Newstead, loveyolk.com.au Felix for Goodness Hiding in plain sight on Burnett Lane in the CBD, this sustainably minded exposed brick and timber cafe remains as vital as ever.



Felix for Goodness in Brisbane City. The all-day brunch menu features a potato and chorizo cutlet, a spiced jackfruit toastie and vanilla pancakes. Where to enjoy it all? A morning slot here at the hight open window overlooking the laneway outside is rite-of-passage stuff. Good to know: The Felix team recently opened Riffe for Goodness in the

storied spot once occupied by Sourced Grocer. 50 Burnett Lane, Brisbane, felixforgoodness.com Sarni



Best sandwich shop in town? Sarni is an absolute contender. A smoked brisket sandwich at Sarni. Markus Ravik The brainchild of Marty Coard, Mat Drummond, Noam Lissner and Hugo

Hirst, Sarni emerged in an unfussy, bright blue space on Racecourse Road in 2024. The menu? A tight set of sandwiches, all of which are served on either a slow-fermented bun or focaccia (both house-made), but that otherwise rotate regularly. Typical proteins are pork, and an Angus brisket that’s brined for seven days, then smoked. Coffee is Bellissimo served espresso and in Vietnamese iced coffees. Good to know: Marty Coard, Mat Drummond and Noam Lissner also own Ach, a cracking Middle Eastern restaurant in Hamilton. 143 Racecourse Rod, Ascot, instagram.com/sarni.bne



Eat at Billy’s Eat at Billy’s sandwiches were an immediate hit when it opened in early

2023 – particularly its take on a reuben, which throws together 150 grams of wood-smoked wagyu brisket pastrami, red cheddar, pickles, and a generous squirt of signature sauce. Eat at Billy’s sandwiches sell out quickly. The masterstroke, though, is the soft, thick-cut white bread used on all the sandwiches – it soaks up any excess sauciness and makes them a cinch to eat. EaB often sell out super early, meaning you need to hustle to catch a sanger – but they’re so good you’ll hardly care. Good to know: Yes, Eat at Billy’s is the sister business is the exceptional Meat at Billy’s, located just next door.



155 Baroona Road, Paddington, eatatbillys.com.au So What Stereo Walking into this obscurely located Valley spot feels like stumbling into the ultimate retro rumpus room, full of found furniture, mid-century layered pendant lights and vintage JBL speakers. So What Stereo is a retro-styled spot that’s cooking legit Thai brunch. Markus Ravik Owner Kawid “Meek” Brikshavana’s Thai brunch menu is just as vivid: expect Thai-style scramble with coal-grilled tiger prawns and nam prik num; Thai boat

noodles; and khao kai kon served with coal-grilled scotch fillet. For drinks, there’s Single O espresso and filter coffee, and chilled drinks such as iced coconut matcha.



Good to know: Thursday through Saturday, the cafe operates at night as

Kasem Sook Social, serving Thai street-style food and natural wines. 4/15 Little Street, Fortitude Valley, instagram.com/so.what.stereo Beurre Pastries Beurre opened mid-2023 and straightaway had inner-west locals lining up

for owner-patissier William Leung’s imaginative spins on classic pastries. Beurre Pastries in Milton. Morgan Roberts.



You might order a smoky cauliflower and bonito Danish, a black sesame and yuzu morning bun, or a caramel brownie pain Suisse. Coffee is Bear Bones. The setting is a slick glass-enclosed spot with stone gardens, the day’s pastries displayed on an eye-catching granite counter. Good to know: Go early if you can – Leung often begins to sell out of

product well before closing time. 33 Park Road, Milton, instagram.com/beurrepastriesbne Salud Salud finds chef Vince Estacio (formerly Naim) leaning into the Latin American cuisine on which he cut his teeth in his native San Francisco more than a decade ago.



Salud cafe & restaurant in Auchenflower. Expect dishes such as a wet burrito smothered in salsa verde sauce and melted cheese, chorizo patatas bravas, and a Latin-inflected shakshuka. The digs, in old Queenslander-style digs on Haig Road, account for the rest of the charm. Coffee is by Campos. Good to know: Salud has one of the best dining backyards in the city

(perfect for functions). 109 Haig Road, Auchenflower, saludbne.com.au Goodfolk Cafe



Great suburban cafes aren’t meant to have a second life but Goodfolk is

arguably better than (the very good) Neighbourhood Coffee Roasters that preceded it in the brilliant old Rainworth General Store space. Goodfolk Cafe in Bardon. Josh Tate Owner Adam Murphy trusts his punters to roll with an imaginative menu that includes Turkish eggs, green eggs topped with lamb rosemary sausage, and dukkah crusted Lebanese lamb meatballs. Neighbourhood lives on by supplying the coffee, and it’s backed by a bunch of teas and house-made juices. Good to know: Goodfolk features a winsome backyard with a produce garden. 58 Rainworth Road, Bardon, goodfolkcafe.com.au



Passport Specialty Coffee This might be the very best. Passport Specialty Coffee in Northgate. The location in a Northgate warehouse is low-key but refined and almost retreat-like, decked out in timber and aggregate concrete floors, with the team pumping out the brews from an enormous coffee bar anchored by a La Marzocco Strada espresso machine. There’s also batch, filter and cold brew available, and blends and equipment for sale on a retail shelf. Good to know: Arguably the best coffee you can get close to the airport,

if you’re chasing a pre- or post-flight brew.



49 Toombul Road, Northgate, passportcoffee.com.au Salt Coffee Roasters Look for the crowd of post-run, pre-shopping Newstead locals on the corner of Doggett Street and Commercial Road and you’ve found Salt Coffee Roasters, Zac Lazarac’s long-term passion project (he used to be a stockbroker) that was finally made manifest in 2019. Tomato flatbread at Salt Coffee Roasters. What started as refined, polished venue built around its custom San Remo coffee machine is a bit more freewheeling these days, but the coffee is first-class and the concise brunch menu on-point, with baked items supplied by Idle.



Good to know: Combine with a visit to newly opened Eclair at the Bay,

which is just across the road. 50 Commercial Road, Newstead, instagram.com/salt.au Bella & Tortie Suzi Unwin’s cherished little bakery that disappeared from Grange in late 2022, before later being reborn in a much more pared back form in Stafford in 2023. Bella & Tortie Markus Ravik



The equation? An unassuming space, stacks of flaky pies and sausage rolls, focaccia sandwiches, and a menu of the best sweets in the business that rotates weekly. An absolute treasure on the north side. Good to know: Open just Friday through Sunday, check B&T’s Instagram for this week’s sweets. Farmhouse There’s nothing subtle about this enormous country-themed shed out at Kedron, but there’s little not to love either, Amanda and John Scott opening Farmhouse in part as a tribute to the Farmer Joe’s produce store, which closed in the same spot in 2009. The OG Breakfast at Farmhouse.



Expect generously sized, produce-driven breakfasts in a rustic space that overflows with verdant greenery. Good to know: Make use of the online bookings because this place

absolutely murders on weekends. 9 Somerset Road, Kedron, farmhousekedron.com.au The Hideout Eddie Cho’s The Hideout is relatively new to the coffee scene but has built a dedicated following on the back of an unfussy, engagement-savvy approach to speciality brews.



The Hideout on Edward Street. He runs three blends at his Edward Street cafe – all produced by Melbourne’s Axil Coffee Roasters – available via espresso and batch brew. There’s also a food menu that’s much better than it needs to be. The handsome white and red cafe itself, with its welcoming alfresco design, accounts for the rest of its charm. Good to know: The Hideout has two other locations, on Adelaide Street in the CBD and St Paul’s Terrace in the Valley. 100 Edward Street, Brisbane, thehideoutspecialtycoffee.com Death Before Decaf



Serving espresso coffee 24-7, 365 days a year is the ultimate excuse to phone it in, but this New Farm institution steadfastly refuses to do so. Death Before Decaf serves coffee 24 hours a day. AFR It’s not uncommon to find taxi drivers and roadworkers gathered around its neon-lit frontage in the depths of a Friday or Saturday night. The shop’s blends, AAA and Roadie – custom-made by local roasters – are bracing for that reason, but the coffee’s always exactingly poured, making this a cherished beacon for serious coffee drinkers. Good to know: The shop itself is a charming spot. Inspired by tattoo and

skate culture, it stocks beans and coffee pods, and hardcore or metal is

always playing. 760-766 Brunswick Street, New Farm, deathbeforedecaf.com.au



Eclair at the Bay Michelin-trained Pavel Stolarsky’s pastry skills are on full display at this

beautiful little shopfront on Commercial Road, which, as you might expect, specialises in immaculately presented eclairs, but also protuberant profiteroles, textural craquelins, and immaculately styled tarts. Eclair at the Bay's white chocolate ganache tart with raspberry coulis. Markus Ravik For drinks, it’s simple: black coffee, tea and fresh-pressed juices. Otherwise, there’s a shelf full of merch, imported candy, books and the like. A very welcome Byron Bay-import. Good to know: Stolarsky and partner Mary Martin also do a buzzing trade in event cakes, including show-stopping croquembouche.



58 Commercial Road, Newstead, eclairatthebay.com Kimino This Ashgrove cafe is all about detail, Kyoto-born owner Mine Hirayama, a pour-over obsessive. Kimino in Ashgrove. Hirayama usually runs three four roasters at anyone time, usually sourced from Japan. There’s also house-baked sweets such as sable cookies and raisin butter sandos, and this beguiling, light- filled cafe’s ceremonial grade matcha is regularly rated as some of the best in town.



Good to know: Kimino is worth visiting for its curated selection of fancy Japanese ceramics alone. 71 Wardell Street, Ashgrove, instagram.com/kimino__bne Honourable Mentions Scout – One of Brisbane’s most beguiling cafes still serves bagels you should care about. Foster & Black – This chain boasts a slick roastery and cafe HQ in the Valley.



Time & Temp – Precision baked pastries and filter coffee in the old Brewbakers spot in Albion. Blue Bear Coffeehouse – this unassuming corner cafe on James Street serves breakfasts locals in the know swear by. Rise Bakery – find first-class French-style pastries at this Newstead and Portside spot. Riffe for Goodness – the Felix for Goodness crew take on Teneriffe in the old Sourced Grocer premises. Dicki’s – a fabulous plant-based cafe that’s hugely popular with New Farm locals.



Dopo Eatery – the old Tognini’s in Milton gets a light and bright refresh. The Single Guys – it might not be pushing any boundaries, but this Kenmore classic is just as charming as ever. Method to the Madness – By now a Kenmore favourite because of its ambitious brunch menu. This and That – It’s all about location at this New Farm cafe in a quaint old Queenslander. Naim – This Paddington cafe’s Middle Eastern-inspired brunches remain a local favourite.



Joe’s Famous Deli – One of the movers and shakers in Brisbane’s fancy sandwich craze. Queen Amann – A slick King Street bakery dedicated to kouign-amann. Wolff Coffee Roasters – Beautifully presented roastery in a handsome Hendra warehouse. Fonzie Abbott – An Albion classic overlooking bucolic Crosby Park. Pancha – Ascot and Hamilton locals flock here for hearty breakfasts and Campos coffee.



Jocelyn’s Provisions – The storied bakeshop remains a James Street and Albion favourite. Brolly Coffee – The Botanica team is behind this beautiful Red Hill coffee shop. James Street Bakery – The engine of James Street Market serves a cracking selection of sourdough. Doughcraft – One of the CBD’s best bakeries transforms into an Italian restaurant at night. Priorities – A brilliant little coffee shack on a grassy strip in Alderley.



Hussk – This cracking Grange cafe boasts some Michelin-trained cred in the kitchen. Sippy Tom – An inviting bolthole slotted beneath the Winchcombe Carson Woolstores. Mr Valentine – Allpress espresso and Doughcraft pastries in a buzzy Valley spot. Supernice – This hidden Bowen Hills gem serves some of the best sandwiches in the area. Blackout Paddington – There are few Paddington coffee spots more popular with locals.



Fave Specialty Coffee – A McLachlan Street gem with precision coffee and a surprisingly refined food menu. The Tiller Coffee – Semi-Pro espresso out of a bright orange shipping container in Alderley. Neighbourhood Coffee Roasters – A beautiful warehouse cafe and roastery in the Albion Fine Trades precinct. Danny’s Bread – Some of the best loaves in Brisbane’s north can be found in this Commercial Road hole in the wall.

World.title: Google hit with $1.5 billion fine over app store, search breaches
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesRegulation Google hit with $1.5 billion fine over app store, search breaches Foo Yun Chee July 23, 2026 — 9:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alphabet’s Google was fined a total of €890 million ($1.45 billion) on Thursday for flouting European Union rules aimed at reining in the power of Big Tech, the European Commission said. However, the US tech giant is likely to avoid fresh fines as EU regulators lauded good progress in its ongoing efforts to comply with the landmark legislation. The fines underscored Europe’s determination to prevent Big Tech companies from thwarting rivals, defying US criticism and retaliatory tariff threats. One of the two fines was for Google’s favouring of its own services in shopping, hotels, transport and sports in search results. Getty Images One fine of €460 million ($750 million) was handed out to Google by the European Commission under the Digital Markets Act for favouring its own services in shopping, hotels, transport and sports results in search results.



A second fine of €430 million ($700 million) targeted Google’s restrictions on its app store Google Play that prevented app developers from steering users free of charge to cheaper offers on rival app stores or websites. Related Article Opinion

Regulation The $3 billion bomb: Apple and co are under attack Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The fines are the first for the US tech giant under the DMA but the fifth and sixth overall for anti-competitive practices, making for total penalties of €10.38 billion ($17 billion) over nearly two decades. “Our duty and obligation is to comply with the laws, that our laws are fully respected,” EU antitrust chief Teresa Ribera told reporters when asked about US pushback. “The DMA is to make sure we have a fair and level playing field. With these decisions we want to make sure there is competition,” EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen told reporters.



Google, which has 60 days to comply with the Commission’s orders to treat rivals in a fair and non-discriminatory manner and to allow app developers to steer users away from its app store, criticised the EU findings and said it might take the Commission to court. “To comply, we are having to strip away real-time Search features Europeans love - like instant pricing and direct availability for hotels, flights, and restaurants - and dismantle safety protections on Google Play,” Google President of Global Affairs Kent Walker said in a statement. “This isn’t fair competition; it’s product degradation driven by a small group of self-serving complainants, with European businesses and consumers taking the hit. Regulation should improve products, not make them worse,” he said. More fines unlikely given ‘constructive dialogue’ The Commission, which acts as the EU competition enforcer, pointed to a “constructive dialogue” with Google and significant progress made to comply with the DMA, indicating that daily penalties for non-compliance are likely off the table.



“Google has proposed and started testing changes to how it presents its own services on Google Search for free services such as shopping, hotels and flights,” the Commission said, calling it substantial progress. Related Article Regulation Apple and Meta hit with €700 million fines in Europe under new digital rules “The Commission also notes that Google has proposed and started testing changes to how it presents shopping ads and content related services, such as sports,” it said, adding it would assess the changes and continue talks with Google. The EU watchdog also said Google may apply the principles of Thursday’s decision to its AI-generated summaries known as AI Overviews and AI Mode and that talks would continue to this end. Google’s changes to its steering terms on Google Play received a tentative thumbs up from the Commission.



“These constitute good progress towards compliance and will also be assessed in light of the cease and desist order of today’s decision,” it said. Europe’s crackdown on Big Tech has angered US President Donald Trump’s administration, which has threatened to retaliate with tariffs for what he said are moves targeting US companies while US lawmakers have also piled on the pressure. The fines are the third under the DMA after penalties handed out to Apple and Meta Platforms in April last year.
